name: मोक्षसंन्यासयोग
teaching: The whole Gita returns in a final spiral: act, but release the fruit; honour your own dharma, even done imperfectly, over another's done well; let devotion carry what effort cannot. Then the teaching ends as all true teaching must — 'thus I have declared it; reflect fully, and do as you choose.' And when every support fails, the last word: abandon all dharmas, take refuge in Me alone; do not grieve. Everything converges: renunciation redefined as release of fruit, work itself made worship, every secret crowned by the final one — abandon all supports and come; I will carry it all. The student stands, the teaching ends in freedom, and where God and human effort ride together, victory is certain.
questions: What is your svadharma — the work that is yours even when done imperfectly?
Krishna ends with 'do as you choose.' What does it mean that the Gita's last move is to return your freedom?
Having walked all eighteen chapters: what, now, will you actually do — like Arjuna, whose final words are 'my doubt is gone; I will act'?

verses.explanation: The final chapter opens with the question beneath all the others: saṁnyāsa and tyāga — renouncing acts versus renouncing within acts — pṛthak, told apart. It is chapter 1's dilemma matured: Arjuna once wanted to walk away from the war; now he asks, with a scholar's precision, what walking away even means. The Gita's whole summation will unfold from this distinction.
verses.connection: The last question — refining ch5's sannyasa-vs-karma-yoga debate into its final form.
verses.reflection: Bring your oldest question to its mature form today: not 'should I quit?' but 'what is quitting?'
verses.background: The final chapter opens with Arjuna's last question, the one the whole dialogue began with in another form: I wish to know the truth of sannyasa and of tyaga, O mighty-armed — renunciation and relinquishment, severally.
verses.hook: What is the difference between renouncing action and renouncing its fruits?

views.text: Arjuna wants the real meaning of the words sannyāsa and tyāga, each as distinct from the other, because their use in earlier chapters was not explicit. Keśi was a demon in horse form whom Vāsudeva killed.

Arjuna's real question is whether sannyasa and tyaga are synonyms or two different things; if different, he wants each nature, if the same, their one nature explained. Both are enjoined in scripture as means to release.
The question arises because earlier chapters praised both the man of relinquishment (2.50) and the man of renunciation (6.1), so Arjuna wants their difference made clear.

The eighteenth chapter gathers the whole Gita under the division of renunciation and relinquishment; Arjuna asks how giving up action and doing action with fruit given up can both be taught without contradiction.
Arjuna asks Krishna to slay his doubt as he slew the demon Keshi. The final chapter sums up the Gita, ending in loving devotion to God as life's highest duty.

verses.explanation: Two clean definitions: saṁnyāsa drops the kāmya — the optional, appetite-driven projects; tyāga keeps acting but drops the fruit of *everything*. views.text: Whether one says 'giving up desire-prompted acts' or 'giving up fruit', both words come down to one sense, giving up; they are not distinct categories like pot and cloth. Even daily duties have results, which is why their fruit can be given up.
The two words are used as synonyms; the decisive teaching that follows concerns tyaga alone, meaning the relinquishment of fruit of all acts, desire-prompted, daily and occasional.
The discerning mean only the giving up of fruit of all works, desire-prompted, daily and occasional, not giving up the works themselves.
Both words at root mean 'to give up' and convey one idea with a slight distinction; he also distinguishes the renunciation of the knower from that taken up in order to reflect on Vedanta.
Some learned people see renunciation as giving up desire-driven works, while the wise stress inner renunciation: doing prescribed duties while giving up desire for their fruits.

refs.note: The Vedas forbid harming any being, yet also prescribe fire sacrifice; one school argues the specific command overrides the general one.

views.text: The first view is the Sankhyas': all action binds, so give it up, or give it up as one gives up passions. The whole debate concerns only those still fit for rites, not knowers who have gone beyond them.

Takes doṣavat narrowly: only action tainted by injury is to be dropped, not all auspicious action, a Sankhya-leaning view; the Mimamsakas reply that scripturally enjoined sacrificial killing is no injury at all.
The Sankhyas argue that every act done with materials involves some harm, so all action binds and must be dropped; the verse states their view only to refute it.
One school says all action breeds desire and harm and should be dropped; another holds that prescribed duties like sacrifice, charity and penance must never be abandoned.

verses.explanation: Niścayam — *my settled conclusion*: the teacher steps forward from the survey to rule. views.text: Krishna uses tyaga as meaning the same as sannyasa. That this giving up is threefold by tamas and the rest holds only for the unenlightened who are still fit for rites, which is why only the Lord can settle it.
The three kinds already taught are relinquishing the fruit, relinquishing possessiveness over the act, and relinquishing one's own agency by ascribing it to the Lord.
Do not think tyaga is commonplace and needs no hearing: it is hard to grasp, and the wise have classed it three ways, as the following verses show.

Renunciation is the basis of a higher life: dropping lower desires and actions for higher ones. Calling Arjuna a tiger among men, Krishna hints it takes courage, truly shown by leaving Maya for devotion.

verses.explanation: The first half of the verdict: the three great acts stay — kāryam eva, emphatically to be done. Their defense is functional: pāvanāni, they *purify*; giving loosens the fist, worship loosens the ego, discipline loosens the appetites. Even manīṣiṇām, the wise, still need the scrubbing. No stage of the path outgrows generosity.

views.text: The wise whom these acts purify are those who do not seek results for themselves.
These acts are to be done daily until death; for those given to contemplation, which is worship, they wash away the past karma that obstructs it.
Purifiers here means they make the mind clean (citta-śuddhi) for those who discriminate.
Uplifting acts must never be renounced. Like a caterpillar's cocoon they may seem binding, but they purify us from within and help us break free.

verses.explanation: The complete formula, signed with full authority — niścitaṁ matam uttamam: do the works, drop two things from inside them — saṅga, the clutch of 'mine', and phala, the claim on outcome. Action's body kept, action's ego removed. This is not a new topic but the promised verdict of 18.4 delivered: all that the earlier chapters taught about action, distilled into one sentence.
verses.connection: The Gita's thesis in final form: 2.47 and 5.10, restated as the Lord's settled verdict.
verses.reflection: Apply the final formula to one task today: do it fully, with attachment and fruit removed from inside it.

views.text: 'Even these' means the very purifying acts just named: though they bind one who is attached, a seeker of liberation must still do them with attachment and hankering for fruit given up. The verse concludes 18.4's promise rather than opening a new topic.
Sacrifice, gift and austerity are to be done until death as worship of the Lord, giving up possessiveness toward both the acts and their fruits.
Saṅga here is the fixed notion 'I am the doer'; the acts are to be done purely as worship of the Lord, with that notion and the fruits both given up.
Good acts should be done in devotion to God, or at least as duty without wanting reward, like a mother nursing her child or a cow giving milk, selfless and therefore sacred.

verses.explanation: The grading of quitting begins at the bottom: dropping niyata karma — the duties woven into one's station and relationships — out of mohāt, confusion about what duty even is. The seeker who abandons dependents for 'detachment', the soldier who deserts calling it peace: renunciation as a fog mistaking itself for a summit.

verses.reflection: Check one abandoned duty for fog — was that renunciation, or confusion wearing its robe?

views.text: For the unenlightened seeker, giving up obligatory duty is unjustified because it is what purifies him. To call a duty binding and then drop it is self-contradictory, which is delusion, and delusion is tamas.

Obligatory acts sustain the body and purify the mind through food offered in sacrifice, and so lead to knowledge; dropping them in the false belief that they bind is erroneous knowledge rooted in tamas.
Dropping desire-prompted acts is right since they bind, but obligatory acts lead to liberation through purity of mind; to give up what should be kept is delusion itself.
Dropping prohibited acts or desire for rewards is right, but abandoning prescribed duties is foolish. Duties purify the mind and build discipline; quitting them degrades the soul.

views.text: The fruit such a person misses is liberation, which follows from renouncing all action as a result of knowledge.
Fearing the effort of gathering materials and the strain of rites, one drops them to pursue knowledge alone; since that is not what scripture means, the fruit, the rise of knowledge, does not come.
Pain belongs to rajas; dropping duty because it hurts, without the insight that the self is not the doer, yields none of the steadiness in knowledge that true relinquishment brings.
Spiritual progress adds responsibility rather than escape. Arjuna did not change his work after the Gita; he changed his consciousness, doing it as devotion to God.

views.text: Even the hope that duty will purify the mind or avert sin is a fruit to be dropped. Ranking it beside the condemned giving up of acts praises this inner relinquishment, which readies the mind for knowledge.
Daily and occasional rites done for their own sake as worship of the Lord, without possessiveness or fruit, are sattvic because sattva gives knowledge of things as they really are.
The mind of one who does duty without agency or selfishness is purified and becomes fit for steadiness in knowledge; this is the Gita's central teaching.
The highest renunciation keeps doing duty while dropping attachment to results. Outward renunciation first breeds hypocrisy; first cultivate inner detachment, then renounce outwardly.

verses.essence: The relinquisher pervaded by sattva, wise, whose doubts are severed, hates not disagreeable work nor clings to the agreeable.
verses.translation: The man of renunciation, pervaded by purity, intelligent, and with his doubts cut asunder, does not hate a disagreeable work nor is he attached to an agreeable one.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + कुशल (good, agreeable): what is not agreeable
सत्त्व (clarity) + समाविष्ट (pervaded): pervaded by sattva
छिन्न (cut) + संशय (doubt): one whose doubts are cut away

verses.explanation: The portrait of the sattvic relinquisher: the inner seesaw stilled — pleasant tasks no longer courted, unpleasant ones no longer dodged; the work is simply what is in front of the hands. Chinna-saṁśayaḥ, doubts severed: the long argument with one's own duty, which began on this very battlefield, finally quiet.
verses.connection: What 18.9's tyaga feels like from inside: the end of the like/dislike negotiation with one's work.
verses.reflection: Spend a day off the seesaw: neither dodging the unpleasant task nor courting the pleasant one.
verses.background: Krishna settles the old dispute by definition and verdict: sages call sannyasa the giving up of desire-prompted acts, tyaga the giving up of the fruit of all acts. Some say all action should be abandoned as evil; others exempt sacrifice, gift, and austerity. Hear My settled judgment: acts of sacrifice, gift, and austerity must not be abandoned — they purify the wise; but even these are to be done releasing attachment and fruit. The threefold tyaga is graded: from delusion, tamasic; from fear of bodily trouble, rajasic; duty done with attachment and fruit renounced, sattvic.
verses.hook: How does a truly detached person face pleasant and unpleasant work?

views.text: Akuśala means desire-prompted rites that bring rebirth, kuśala the daily duties; he neither hates the one nor is attached to the other. Purified by karma-yoga, he realizes the actionless Self and gives up all action mentally.

Filled with sattva and right knowledge, he renounces all results other than Brahman and the sense of agency, so he neither loves acts that bring worldly prosperity nor hates those that bring harm; abandonment means this, not giving up acts.

Gives homely examples: he does not resent a cold dawn bath in winter nor relish a midday bath in summer, because one who bears great hardship for a higher aim weighs such passing pleasure and pain as nothing.
Sattvic renouncers do their duty calmly in good and bad times, bending like reeds with the waves. Tilak's calm amid arrest and his son's illness shows such composure.

verses.devanagari:
न हि देहभृता शक्यं त्यक्तुं कर्माण्यशेषतः ।
यस्तु कर्मफलत्यागी स त्यागीत्यभिधीयते॥
verses.transliteration:
na hi dehabhṛtā śakyaṃ tyaktuṃ karmāṇyaśeṣataḥ
yastu karmaphalatyāgī sa tyāgītyabhidhīyate
verses.essence: For an embodied being cannot relinquish actions entirely; but one who relinquishes the fruit of action — that one is called the relinquisher.
verses.translation: Verily, it is not possible for an embodied being to abandon actions entirely; but he who relinquishes the rewards of actions is verily called a man of renunciation.

anvaya.meaning: by one who bears a body
anvaya.parts: देह (body) + भृत् (bearer): one who bears a body

anvaya.form: gerundive, neuter, nominative singular (can be done)

anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + फल (fruit) + त्यागिन् (giver-up): one who gives up the fruit of action

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is called)

verses.explanation: The decisive realism: na hi dehabhṛtā śakyam — a body *is* action; breath, digestion, the beat of the heart never resign. Total quitting is not renunciation but a fiction (3.5's old point, now final doctrine). So the title 'tyāgī' is formally reassigned: not the one who does nothing, but the one who keeps nothing — karma-phala-tyāgī, the fruit-releaser.
verses.connection: Closes the definitional question of 18.1 with anatomy: only the fruit can be fully renounced.
verses.reflection: Stop attempting the impossible renunciation today — breath and heartbeat never resign. Release fruits instead.
verses.background: Krishna settles the old dispute by definition and verdict: sages call sannyasa the giving up of desire-prompted acts, tyaga the giving up of the fruit of all acts. Some say all action should be abandoned as evil; others exempt sacrifice, gift, and austerity. Hear My settled judgment: acts of sacrifice, gift, and austerity must not be abandoned — they purify the wise; but even these are to be done releasing attachment and fruit. The threefold tyaga is graded: from delusion, tamasic; from fear of bodily trouble, rajasic; duty done with attachment and fruit renounced, sattvic.
verses.hook: Can anyone with a body ever stop acting altogether?

views.text: The 'body-bearer' is the unenlightened one who identifies with the body; for him total renunciation is impossible, so calling the fruit-relinquisher a tyagi is praise. Full renunciation belongs only to one who has realized the Self.

Eating and drinking to sustain the body cannot be dropped, so neither can the great daily sacrifices; giving up fruit here implies giving up agency and attachment too, the three kinds announced in 18.4.

Real relinquishment is action done by knowers of Brahman without desire for fruit, even-minded in success and failure; strictly the word fits only a sage who has let go of his hold on the three gunas.
Total inactivity is impossible for the embodied, since eating, breathing and thinking go on. Giving up attachment to the fruits of action is therefore perfect renunciation.

verses.devanagari:
अनिष्टमिष्टं मिश्रं च त्रिविधं कर्मणः फलम् ।
भवत्यत्यागिनां प्रेत्य न तु संन्यासिनां क्वचित्॥
verses.transliteration:
aniṣṭamiṣṭaṃ miśraṃ ca trividhaṃ karmaṇaḥ phalam
bhavatyatyāgināṃ pretya na tu saṃnyāsināṃ kvacit
verses.essence: Unwished, wished, and mixed — threefold is the fruit of action that accrues after death to the non-relinquishers; but never to the renouncers.
verses.translation: The threefold fruit of action (evil, good and mixed) accrues after death to the non-abandoners, but never to the abandoners.

anvaya.parts: अन् (not) + इष्ट (desired): what is not wished for
त्रि (three) + विधा (kind): of three kinds

anvaya.base: अत्यागिन् · one who does not give up
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + त्यागिन् (relinquisher): those who do not relinquish

verses.explanation: The stakes across the death-line: for the grasper, every deed ripens — sweet, bitter, or the usual blend — and the harvest follows into the hereafter. For the fruit-releaser: na tu... kvacit, *never, anywhere*. Not because their deeds vanish, but because nothing was planted in the soil of 'mine'. An open hand, it turns out, is the only place karma cannot take root.
verses.connection: The metaphysical payoff of 18.11: the released fruit never returns to bind.
verses.reflection: Plant nothing in the soil of 'mine' today, and notice there is nothing to harvest you later.
verses.background: Krishna settles the old dispute by definition and verdict: sages call sannyasa the giving up of desire-prompted acts, tyaga the giving up of the fruit of all acts. Some say all action should be abandoned as evil; others exempt sacrifice, gift, and austerity. Hear My settled judgment: acts of sacrifice, gift, and austerity must not be abandoned — they purify the wise; but even these are to be done releasing attachment and fruit. The threefold tyaga is graded: from delusion, tamasic; from fear of bodily trouble, rajasic; duty done with attachment and fruit renounced, sattvic.
verses.hook: What happens after death to the results of your actions?

views.text: The renouncers spared all fruit are paramahamsa monks steadfast in knowledge alone, who have dug out the seed of rebirth; total renunciation is possible only for those who know the supreme Truth.

Those who give up agency, possessiveness and fruit meet no results opposed to release; the same rites, applied toward release rather than desire, bear a different fruit. Pretya can also mean 'after the act'.
Saṃnyāsin here includes the fruit-relinquishers just described, as in 6.1; for such sattvic people sin does not arise and merit is offered to the Lord, so no threefold fruit comes.
Desire-driven actions bring heavenly, hellish or mixed human births after death. When personal motive is given up and work is done as duty to God, no such results accrue.

verses.devanagari:
पञ्चैतानि महाबाहो कारणानि निबोध मे ।
साङ्ख्ये कृतान्ते प्रोक्तानि सिद्धये सर्वकर्मणाम्॥
verses.transliteration:
pañcaitāni mahābāho kāraṇāni nibodha me
sāṅkhye kṛtānte proktāni siddhaye sarvakarmaṇām
verses.essence: Learn from me, Mahabaho, these five causes for the accomplishment of all action, declared in the Sankhya doctrine where actions reach their end.
verses.translation: Learn from Me, O mighty-armed Arjuna, these five causes as declared in the Sankhya system for the accomplishment of all actions.

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + बाहु (arm): one whose arms are mighty

anvaya.meaning: in which action reaches its end
anvaya.base: कृतान्त · final doctrine, end of action
anvaya.parts: कृत (action, what is done) + अन्त (end): that in which actions come to an end

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter, accusative plural (declared)

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + कर्मन् (action): all actions

verses.explanation: A new analysis opens: if the fruit must be released, the *authorship* must be understood. The Sankhya — the science where action's accounting is settled — is summoned to dissect a single question: when something gets done, who actually did it? Five causes are about to replace the one proud claimant.
verses.connection: Begins the doership-audit (18.13–17): the final dismantling of 'I did this'.
verses.reflection: Audit one accomplishment today for its real causes — prepare to find five names on the invoice.
verses.background: The anatomy of action is laid out from Sankhya doctrine: five factors in every deed — the body-seat, the doer, the instruments, the various functions, and providence as the fifth. Seeing this, whoever beholds the self as sole doer sees not. He whose state is free of the ego-notion, though he slay these worlds, slays not and is not bound. Knowledge, the known, and the knower impel action; instrument, act, and agent comprise it.
verses.hook: What does Krishna say makes up any action?

views.text: Sāṅkhya here means Vedanta, where what is to be known is fully stated, and kṛtānta means that in which all actions culminate, since knowledge of the Self ends action (2.46, 4.33).

Sāṅkhya means buddhi: what reason settles in line with the Vedas about things as they are. That Vedic understanding holds the Supreme Self, the Inner Ruler, to be the agent working through body, senses, breath and self.

Offers both readings: the knowledge of the Supreme as the Vedanta conclusion, or the Sankhya system where principles are enumerated; either way the five are taught to remove the self's pride of doership.
To deepen detachment Krishna explains the parts of action, an analysis already found in Sankhya, the philosophy of Kapila that studies the elements of body, world and cause and effect.

verses.devanagari:
अधिष्ठानं तथा कर्ता करणं च पृथग्विधम् ।
विविधाश्च पृथक्चेष्टा दैवं चैवात्र पञ्चमम्॥
verses.transliteration:
adhiṣṭhānaṃ tathā kartā karaṇaṃ ca pṛthagvidham
vividhāśca pṛthakceṣṭā daivaṃ caivātra pañcamam
verses.essence: The seat of action, the agent, the various instruments, the manifold distinct efforts, and divine providence as the fifth —
verses.translation: The seat (body), the doer, the various senses, the different functions of various sorts, and the presiding deity, also, the fifth.

anvaya.base: अधिष्ठान · base, seat (अधि + √स्था · to stand on)

anvaya.parts: पृथक् (separate) + विधा (kind): of separate kinds

verses.explanation: The five factors of every deed: the body as platform; the apparent agent; the instruments — senses, tools, hands; the many energies actually exerting; and daivam, the fifth — the divine: for the classical commentators the powers presiding over the senses or the Lord within, and for many readers providence, everything in the outcome that no one controls. Any honest audit of any accomplishment finds all five on the invoice.
verses.connection: The cast list behind every act — drawn up so 18.16 can expose the one false credit.
verses.reflection: Honor the fifth factor once today: daivam — the part of every outcome no one controlled.
verses.background: The anatomy of action is laid out from Sankhya doctrine: five factors in every deed — the body-seat, the doer, the instruments, the various functions, and providence as the fifth. Seeing this, whoever beholds the self as sole doer sees not. He whose state is free of the ego-notion, though he slay these worlds, slays not and is not bound. Knowledge, the known, and the knower impel action; instrument, act, and agent comprise it.
verses.hook: What are the five factors behind every action?

refs.note: It is the soul that sees, touches, hears, tastes, thinks and understands; it is both knower and doer, one factor of action.
It is truly the soul that is the knower.
The soul is the doer of actions, as scripture confirms, so the agent is a real cause.

views.text: The agent is the individual self that seems to take on the traits of its adjuncts; daivam is the Sun and other deities presiding over the eye and the other organs.
The agent is the individual self, a real knower and doer, but daivam, the fifth, is the Supreme Self as Inner Ruler, the main cause in completing any act; the self's agency depends on Him.
The doer is ahaṃkāra, the knot tying consciousness to matter; daivam is either the Sun and other powers that assist the senses or the Inner Ruler who moves all.
Action needs the body, the soul as doer, the senses, effort, and God, who gives each person abilities based on past karma and grants results.

verses.devanagari:
शरीरवाङ्मनोभिर्यत्कर्म प्रारभते नरः ।
न्याय्यं वा विपरीतं वा पञ्चैते तस्य हेतवः॥
verses.transliteration:
śarīravāṅmanobhiryatkarma prārabhate naraḥ
nyāyyaṃ vā viparītaṃ vā pañcaite tasya hetavaḥ
verses.essence: Whatever action a person undertakes by body, speech and mind, whether right or contrary — these five are its causes.
verses.translation: Whatever action a man performs with his body, speech and mind whether right or the reverse these five are its causes.

anvaya.base: शरीर · body; वाच् · speech; मनस् · mind
anvaya.form: noun, neuter, instrumental plural (by means of)
anvaya.parts: शरीर (body) + वाच् (speech) + मनस् (mind): body, speech and mind together

verses.explanation: The audit's scope declared total: every deed through any door — body, speech, mind — and of any moral color, nyāyyaṁ vā viparītaṁ vā, righteous or its opposite. No act anywhere escapes the five-fold causation; the saint's service and the thief's theft are both committee productions. Which makes the next verse's lone claimant absurd.
verses.connection: Universalizes 18.14's five causes — setting the trap for the solitary 'I'.
verses.reflection: Extend the audit everywhere: body, speech, mind; right deeds and wrong — all are committee work.
verses.background: The anatomy of action is laid out from Sankhya doctrine: five factors in every deed — the body-seat, the doer, the instruments, the various functions, and providence as the fifth. Seeing this, whoever beholds the self as sole doer sees not. He whose state is free of the ego-notion, though he slay these worlds, slays not and is not bound. Knowledge, the known, and the knower impel action; instrument, act, and agent comprise it.
verses.hook: Whatever you do in body, speech or mind, what causes it?

refs.note: Speech, mind, eyes, ears and breath work only by the power of Brahman, which they cannot reach; so the self is not the sole doer.

views.text: 'Right or its reverse' covers even instinctive acts like blinking, as effects of past merit and demerit. Body, speech and mind are named because every act and its fruit runs chiefly through one of the three.
Whether an act is enjoined or forbidden by scripture, the same five causes operate, with the Supreme Self, the Inner Ruler, as the fifth and chief cause on whom the individual self's agency depends.
All acts of body, speech and mind, good or bad, arise from five causes. Seeing this dissolves the ego's claim to be the sole doer.

verses.devanagari:
तत्रैवं सति कर्तारमात्मानं केवलं तु यः ।
पश्यत्यकृतबुद्धित्वान्न स पश्यति दुर्मतिः॥
verses.transliteration:
tatraivaṃ sati kartāramātmānaṃ kevalaṃ tu yaḥ
paśyatyakṛtabuddhitvānna sa paśyati durmatiḥ
verses.essence: That being so, one who sees the self alone as the doer — through unrefined understanding — that perverse-minded one does not truly see.
verses.translation: Now, such being the case, verily he who owing to untrained understanding looks upon his Self, which is isolated, as the agent, he of perverted intelligence, sees not.

anvaya.form: present participle, locative singular ('this being so')

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + कृत (made, refined) + बुद्धि (understanding) + त्व (-ness): the state of having an unrefined understanding
दुस् (bad) + मति (mind): one whose mind is wrong

verses.explanation: The exposure: with five causes on record, crediting kevalam ātmānam — the bare self, alone — is not pride's harmless flourish but a perceptual error: na sa paśyati, that one *does not see*. Akṛta-buddhitvāt: the instrument of understanding never finished. Every 'I did it single-handedly' is a five-handed event wearing one glove.
verses.connection: The audit's verdict: sole-doership as the root misperception — preparing 18.17's stunning corollary.
verses.reflection: Catch one 'I did it single-handedly' today and count the other four hands.

Seeing this, whoever beholds the self as sole doer sees not. He whose state is free of the ego-notion, though he slay these worlds, slays not and is not bound. Knowledge, the known, and the knower impel action; instrument, act, and agent comprise it.
verses.hook: Why is it a mistake to see yourself as the only doer?

refs.note: Speech, mind, eyes, ears and breath work only by the power of Brahman, which they cannot reach; so the self is not the sole doer.

views.text: Kevalam means the pure, absolute Self: to see that Self as agent, even while knowing it is distinct from the body, is imperfect understanding, like one in a palanquin thinking he moves when the bearers do.
The self's agency exists but depends on the consent of the Supreme Self; one who sees himself as the sole agent does not see how things actually stand.
The Self is the actionless, silent witness; the egoist who thinks he alone is the doer binds himself with karma and is born again to reap it.
The soul steers like a driver, but without a body from God and God's energy it could do nothing. Giving him the credit frees us from doership and lets us act for his pleasure.

verses.devanagari:
यस्य नाहंकृतो भावो बुद्धिर्यस्य न लिप्यते ।
हत्वाऽपि स इमाँल्लोकान्न हन्ति न निबध्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
yasya nāhaṃkṛto bhāvo buddhiryasya na lipyate
hatvā'pi sa imāṃllokānna hanti na nibadhyate
verses.essence: One who is free of the sense 'I am the doer', whose understanding is unstained — though slaying these worlds, such a one slays not, and is not bound.
verses.translation: He who is free from the egoistic notion, whose intelligence is not tainted (by good or evil), though he slays these people, he slayeth not, nor is he bound (by the action).

anvaya.meaning: made by the ego, 'I am the doer'
anvaya.parts: अहम् (I) + कृत (made) — 'made by the I', the notion 'I did it'

verses.explanation: The audit's vertiginous conclusion, aimed straight at the man holding the bow: where the ahaṅkṛta bhāva — the knot of 'I am the agent' — is genuinely absent and the buddhi unstained by the thought 'I did this, I will pay for it', the deed does not adhere. Hatvāpi... na hanti: even slaying, one slays not. Not a loophole but a description of the rarest inner state, seen from the Self that never acted at all; to the eye of the world the killing still happens. The chapter then turns from the doer's freedom to the anatomy of every deed — what impels it, what composes it, and how the gunas colour each part.
verses.connection: Echoes 2.19–21 at the chapter of decision: action without ego leaves no fingerprint.
verses.reflection: Aspire to the unstained state honestly — and notice the verse describes egolessness, never excuses.

Seeing this, whoever beholds the self as sole doer sees not. He whose state is free of the ego-notion, though he slay these worlds, slays not and is not bound. Knowledge, the known, and the knower impel action; instrument, act, and agent comprise it.
verses.hook: How can someone act, even in battle, without being bound by it?

views.text: Two standpoints resolve the paradox: 'even slaying' speaks from the world's view that identifies self with body; 'slays not, is not bound' speaks from the truth that the changeless Self never combines with the five factors of action.
Freedom from the conceit 'I alone do everything' comes from contemplating the Supreme Person as the agent; such a one is not bound by the battle, and its fruits do not accrue to him.
Takes the unstained buddhi as one that does not cling to deeds as wanted or unwanted; he slays by the world's sight but not by his own, seeing the Self as distinct from the body.
Compares such desireless action to an executioner acting for the peace of the community: once selfishness and the sense of agency are gone, the act no longer binds.
A pure intellect is free of pride in doership and seeks no fruits, so it is not bound by karma. Rahim lowered his eyes while giving, knowing the real giver was God.

verses.devanagari:
ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं परिज्ञाता त्रिविधा कर्मचोदना ।
करणं कर्म कर्तेति त्रिविधः कर्मसंग्रहः॥
verses.transliteration:
jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ parijñātā trividhā karmacodanā
karaṇaṃ karma karteti trividhaḥ karmasaṃgrahaḥ
verses.essence: Knowledge, the known and the knower form the threefold impulse to action; the instrument, the act and the agent form the threefold constitution of action.
verses.translation: Knowledge, the knowable and the knower form the threefold impulse to action; the organ, the action and the agent form the threefold basis of action.

anvaya.form: gerundive (to be known), neuter, nominative singular

anvaya.parts: त्रि (three) + विधा (kind) — 'having three kinds'
कर्म (action) + चोदना (impulse) — 'what impels action'

anvaya.form: indeclinable (marks the end of a list)

anvaya.parts: त्रि (three) + विधा (kind) — 'having three kinds'
कर्म (action) + संग्रह (gathering) — 'that in which action is contained'

verses.explanation: The anatomy of any deed, before and after: upstream, the triad that sparks it — something known, someone knowing, the knowing itself; downstream, the triad that constitutes it — instrument, act, agent. Six joints in every action. The chapter now runs its guna-lens over three of them — knowledge, action, agent — and then onward through the whole inner apparatus.
verses.connection: The framework for the great triads (18.19–40): everything human, sorted three ways.
verses.reflection: Watch one act assemble today: known, knower, knowing — then instrument, deed, doer. Six joints, every time.
verses.background: The anatomy of action is laid out from Sankhya doctrine: five factors in every deed — the body-seat, the doer, the instruments, the various functions, and providence as the fifth. Seeing this, whoever beholds the self as sole doer sees not. He whose state is free of the ego-notion, though he slay these worlds, slays not and is not bound. Knowledge, the known, and the knower impel action; instrument, act, and agent comprise it.
verses.hook: What moves a person to act, and what makes up an action?

views.text: Action can begin only when knowledge, object and knower come together; once begun through the five factors, every act is contained in instrument, object and agent — the knower and agent being products of ignorance, not the Self.

Reads the first triad as the Vedic injunction: knowledge of the duty to be done, the duty itself as its object, and the one who knows it; the act is then instrument (materials), action (the sacrifice) and performer.

The same six are one set seen at two moments: in thought they are knowledge, known and knower; when desire for fruit absorbs them they become instrument, object and agent. For the yogin without that absorption they stay only knowledge.
Knowledge, its object and the knower together impel action, as knowledge of pay or gold drives work. The doer, instrument and deed make up action, and all vary with the modes.

verses.devanagari:
ज्ञानं कर्म च कर्ताच त्रिधैव गुणभेदतः ।
प्रोच्यते गुणसङ्ख्याने यथावच्छृणु तान्यपि॥
verses.transliteration:
jñānaṃ karma ca kartāca tridhaiva guṇabhedataḥ
procyate guṇasaṅkhyāne yathāvacchṛṇu tānyapi
verses.essence: Knowledge, action and agent are declared in the doctrine of the gunas to be of three kinds only, according to the difference of the gunas. Hear of them also, duly.
verses.translation: Knowledge, action and actor are declared in the science of the Gunas (Sankhya philosophy) to be of three kinds only, according to the distinction of the Gunas. Of these also, hear duly.

anvaya.meaning: according to the difference of gunas
anvaya.parts: गुण (strand) + भेद (difference) + -तः — 'by the distinction of the gunas'

anvaya.meaning: in the science of the gunas
anvaya.parts: गुण (strand) + सङ्ख्यान (enumeration) — 'the teaching that counts the gunas', i.e. Sāṅkhya

verses.explanation: The program announced: jñāna, karma, kartā — the seeing, the doing, the doer — each refracted through sattva, rajas, tamas. What follows through 18.40 is the Gita's final gift of discernment: a complete field guide to the inner life, nine portraits and more, by which a person can locate, at any hour, which strand currently holds the pen.
verses.connection: Opens the systematic survey that runs to 18.40 — the guna-science completed.
verses.reflection: Carry the field-guide consciously today: your seeing, doing, and doer each have a current grade.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: How do the three modes shape knowledge, action and the doer?

views.text: Kapila's guna-teaching is cited as authoritative on how the gunas work, though not on the non-dual Brahman; 'only' stresses that knowledge, action and agent have no division beyond the gunas.
Each term covers both sides: 'knowledge' means the instruments of both knowing and acting, 'action' their objects, 'agent' both knower and doer — mapping the triads that follow, 18.20–35.
The 'only' shows that agency belongs to the gunas as limiting adjuncts; the Self has no doership of its own.
After showing the modes' role in faith, food and charity, Krishna now applies them to knowledge, action and doers, citing Sankhya as an authority on material nature though it denies the Supreme.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वभूतेषु येनैकं भावमव्ययमीक्षते ।
अविभक्तं विभक्तेषु तज्ज्ञानं विद्धि सात्त्विकम्॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvabhūteṣu yenaikaṃ bhāvamavyayamīkṣate
avibhaktaṃ vibhakteṣu tajjñānaṃ viddhi sāttvikam
verses.essence: That knowledge by which one sees the one imperishable Being in all beings — undivided in the divided — know that knowledge to be sattvic.
verses.translation: That by which one sees the one indestructible Reality in all beings, not separate in all the separate beings know thou that knowledge to be Sattvic.

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + भूत (being) — 'all beings'
अ (not) + व्यय (decay) — 'not subject to decay'
अ (not) + विभक्त (divided) — 'not divided'

verses.explanation: The highest knowing in one image: avibhaktaṁ vibhakteṣu — the undivided seen *within* the divided; one ocean recognized beneath the count of waves. Sattvic knowledge does not deny the many; it sees through them without erasing them — 13.28's vision filed here as the gold standard of cognition itself.
verses.connection: First panel of the knowledge-triad: unity perceived through, not instead of, difference.
verses.reflection: Practice the gold standard of knowing once: the undivided glimpsed inside the divided crowd.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. verses.hook: What kind of knowledge sees one reality in all beings?

refs.note: Knowers of truth say there is one entity without a second, the unity sattvic knowledge sees behind diversity.
Every limb of God's body can perform the functions of every other, showing he is one without internal difference.

views.text: This is full realisation of the non-dual Self: one changeless reality, undivided like space in all bodies; dualist views, being based on rajas and tamas, cannot end worldly existence.
The selves are many yet alike in nature: sattvic knowledge sees the same immutable, knowledge-formed self behind distinctions of caste, stage of life and body.
The one undecaying reality is the supreme Self, threaded through all beings from Brahmā to the unmoving, while those beings stay mutually distinct.
Sattvic knowledge sees the Supreme Lord as the one substratum behind all diversity, like gold in many ornaments. Love born of this vision is universal, not racial or national.

verses.devanagari:
पृथक्त्वेन तु यज्ज्ञानं नानाभावान्पृथग्विधान् ।
वेत्ति सर्वेषु भूतेषु तज्ज्ञानं विद्धि राजसम्॥
verses.transliteration:
pṛthaktvena tu yajjñānaṃ nānābhāvānpṛthagvidhān
vetti sarveṣu bhūteṣu tajjñānaṃ viddhi rājasam
verses.essence: But that knowledge which sees in all beings manifold entities of distinct kinds, each separate — know that knowledge to be rajasic.
verses.translation: But that knowledge which sees in all beings various entities of distinct kinds as different from one another know thou that knowledge to be Rajasic.

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, instrumental singular (by way of)

anvaya.parts: नाना (various) + भाव (entity) — 'various entities'
पृथक् (separate) + विधा (kind) — 'each of its own kind'

verses.explanation: Rajasic knowing: pṛthaktvena, by separateness first and last — each being taken as a self of its own kind, one happy, one wretched, one high, one low, as the body appears; no common thread suspected. It sees the many truly enough as many, but stops at the catalogue, and takes the catalogue for the whole truth. A world of sealed, separate selves is a world to be ranked, compared, and contested.
verses.connection: Second panel: the many seen, the one missed — the cognition that fuels rivalry.
verses.reflection: Notice inventory-vision running today — everything separate, rankable — competent, and blind to the thread.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. verses.hook: What kind of knowledge sees only separate, divided beings?

views.text: Since knowledge itself cannot be an agent, the sense is 'knowledge through which one apprehends' many selves, different from oneself and separate in each body.
Not a condemnation of the plurality of selves: the fault is taking the self to differ in nature because bodies differ in height or colour and in fitness for results of work.
Rajasic seeing sorts beings as gods, humans and so on with the thought 'here lies my pleasure, there my displeasure'.
Knowledge that does not see the world in relation to God sees only plurality of race, class and nation. Knowledge that unites is sattvic; knowledge that divides is rajasic.

verses.devanagari:
यत्तु कृत्स्नवदेकस्मिन्कार्ये सक्तमहैतुकम् ।
अतत्त्वार्थवदल्पं च तत्तामसमुदाहृतम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yattu kṛtsnavadekasminkārye saktamahaitukam
atattvārthavadalpaṃ ca tattāmasamudāhṛtam
verses.essence: But that which clings to one single effect as if it were the whole — without reason, without grasp of truth, and trivial — that is declared tamasic.
verses.translation: But that which clings to one single effect as if it were the whole, without reason, without foundation in Truth, and trivial that is declared to be Tamasic.

anvaya.meaning: as if it were the whole
anvaya.parts: कृत्स्न (whole) + -वत् (like) — 'like the whole'
अ (not) + हैतुक (reasoned) — 'groundless'

anvaya.base: तत्त्वार्थ · the real nature of things
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + तत्त्व (truth) + अर्थ (object) + वत् (having) — 'not having truth as its object'

verses.explanation: Tamasic knowing: one fragment mistaken for everything — kṛtsna-vat ekasmin, the whole world shrunk to a single obsession, grievance, or slogan; held ahaitukam, without reason, immune to evidence; alpam, small, and proud of its smallness. Fanaticism's epistemology in a single verse.
verses.connection: Third panel: the part enthroned as the whole — knowledge collapsed to a keyhole.
verses.reflection: Find where one fragment has become your whole — an obsession, a grievance — and reopen the frame.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: What does narrow knowledge that mistakes a part for the whole look like?

views.text: The 'one effect' is a single body or an image taken as all there is — 'the Self or God is only this much' — knowledge without logic, not aimed at truth, and trivial in its results.
Applies it to work: clinging to one small rite, such as worship of ghosts and spirits, as if it yielded every fruit — groundless, untrue and paltry in result.
'Without reason' means falling slavishly into anger or desire through one's own addiction, never examining the cause.
A dulled intellect clings to a fragment of truth as if it were all and turns fanatical, imposing its views on others and disrupting society in God's name.

verses.devanagari:
नियतं सङ्गरहितमरागद्वेषतः कृतम् ।
अफलप्रेप्सुना कर्म यत्तत्सात्त्विकमुच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
niyataṃ saṅgarahitamarāgadveṣataḥ kṛtam
aphalaprepsunā karma yattatsāttvikamucyate
verses.essence: Action that is ordained, free of attachment, performed without passion or hatred by one not desiring the fruit — that is called sattvic.
verses.translation: An action which is ordained, which is free from attachment, and which is done without love or hatred by one who is not desirous of any reward that action is declared to be Sattvic.

anvaya.parts: सङ्ग (attachment) + रहित (devoid) — 'free of attachment'
अ (not) + राग (liking) + द्वेष (hatred) + -तः — 'not out of love or hate'

anvaya.meaning: by one not craving the fruit
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + फल (fruit) + प्रेप्सु (seeking to get) — 'one who does not seek the fruit'

verses.explanation: The action-triad opens with the deed this whole scripture commends: niyatam, the called-for thing; performed with neither the lean of craving nor the flinch of aversion; the doer aphala-prepsu, not reaching past the act toward its reward. Work as clean as weather — it happens fully, and claims nothing.
verses.connection: The sattvic deed: 18.9's tyaga seen from the action's side.
verses.reflection: Do the called-for thing today without lean or flinch — neither craving the task nor dreading it.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: What makes an action pure and well done?

refs.note: Do not treat others as you would not wish to be treated, and check your conduct against scripture, a measure for right action.
Do to others as you would have them do to you, echoing the Mahābhārata's rule.

views.text: Sattvic action is the daily obligatory work done without attachment or likes and dislikes, by an agent who is the opposite of one desiring the fruits.
'Without attachment' means without the sense of agency; 'without desire or aversion' means not done to win fame or avoid disrepute — work performed without ostentation.
Liking and hatred are concrete here: the act is not done out of love for sons and kin or out of hatred for an enemy.
The pure worker offers the reward willingly at the feet of the Lord and works by the scriptures, and finds great joy in the work itself.
Unlike philosophies of pleasure, self-interest, majority or conscience, the Gita defines action in goodness as duty done by scripture, without attachment, aversion or desire for results.

verses.devanagari:
यत्तु कामेप्सुना कर्म साहंकारेण वा पुनः ।
क्रियते बहुलायासं तद्राजसमुदाहृतम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yattu kāmepsunā karma sāhaṃkāreṇa vā punaḥ
kriyate bahulāyāsaṃ tadrājasamudāhṛtam
verses.essence: But action performed with great strain by one seeking desires, or again with the sense of 'I' — that is declared rajasic.
verses.translation: But that action which is done by one longing for the fulfilment of desires or gain with egoism or with much effort that is declared to be Rajasic (passionate).

anvaya.parts: काम (desire) + ईप्सु (seeking) — 'one who seeks desired things'
स (with) + अहंकार (ego) — 'one with ego'
बहुल (much) + आयास (strain) — 'involving much strain'

verses.explanation: Rajasic action's tell is in the texture: bahulāyāsam, *enormously effortful* — not because the task is large but because the doer is carrying two loads, the work and the self doing the work. Wanting and self-display are heavy. Notice the same deed done sattvic feels lighter; the strain was never in the labor but in the grip.
verses.connection: The straining middle: action freighted with appetite and authorship.
verses.reflection: Feel the double load once today — the work plus the self doing the work — and set down the second.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: What marks action done with strain, ambition and ego?

views.text: 'Egotistic' is not contrasted with the knower of truth but with the ordinary modest Vedic scholar; even the doer of sattvic action, lacking Self-knowledge, still has ego.
'Or' has the sense of 'and': the rajasic act is done for results, with the notion that oneself is the agent, and with the thought 'this enormous effort is all mine'.
The egoism is that of pride in learning: 'who is a Vedic scholar equal to me?'
Passion breeds intense desire, so its actions are driven by ambition and heavy toil. The stress of executives, politicians and anxious parents often shows this kind of work.

verses.devanagari:
अनुबन्धं क्षयं हिंसामनपेक्ष्य च पौरुषम् ।
मोहादारभ्यते कर्म यत्तत्तामसमुच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
anubandhaṃ kṣayaṃ hiṃsāmanapekṣya ca pauruṣam
mohādārabhyate karma yattattāmasamucyate
verses.essence: Action undertaken from delusion, without regard for consequence, loss, injury, or one's own capacity — that is called tamasic.
verses.translation: That action which is undertaken from delusion, without a regard for the consequences, loss, injury and (one's own) ability that is declared to be Tamasic (dark).

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, ablative singular (from, because of)

verses.explanation: Tamasic action: launched mohāt, out of fog, with four blind spots — what follows from it, what it destroys, whom it wounds, and whether one can even carry it. The reckless venture, the cruelty that never imagined its victim, the commitment made by someone who never measured themselves. Action without a single look ahead, behind, or within.
verses.connection: The action-triad closes — and 18.26 turns the lens from the deed to its doer.
verses.reflection: Before one undertaking today, take the four looks: consequence, cost, harm, and your real capacity.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. verses.hook: What is action like when done blindly, without regard for harm?

views.text: Glosses the four: the result that follows later, the loss of energy or wealth spent, suffering caused to creatures, and one's own ability to finish — all ignored out of non-discrimination.
The 'delusion' behind such action is specifically ignoring the agency of the Supreme Person.
Those in ignorance act only for themselves, ignoring right and wrong, resources and others' suffering. Such action wastes time and health, as in gambling, theft or drinking.

verses.devanagari:
मुक्तसङ्गोऽनहंवादी धृत्युत्साहसमन्वितः ।
सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योर्निर्विकारः कर्ता सात्त्विक उच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
muktasaṅgo'nahaṃvādī dhṛtyutsāhasamanvitaḥ
siddhyasiddhyornirvikāraḥ kartā sāttvika ucyate
verses.essence: Free of attachment, without egoism, endowed with steadfastness and zeal, unmoved in success and failure — such an agent is called sattvic.
verses.translation: An agent who is free from attachment, non-egoistic, endowed with firmness and enthusiasm, and unaffected by success or failure, is called Sattvic (pure).

anvaya.parts: मुक्त (released) + सङ्ग (attachment) — 'one whose attachment is released'
अन् (not) + अहम् (I) + वादिन् (speaker) — 'one who does not keep saying I'
धृति (firmness) + उत्साह (zeal) + समन्वित (endowed) — 'endowed with firmness and zeal'
सिद्धि (success) + असिद्धि (failure) — 'success and failure'
निर् (without) + विकार (change) — 'without change'

verses.explanation: The sattvic doer, and the portrait corrects a misreading at once: utsāha-samanvitaḥ — *full of zeal*. Detachment is not lukewarmness; this worker burns with energy and holds with nothing. Anahaṁ-vādī, not speaking in 'I': listen to how someone narrates their work and you hear their strand. Nirvikāraḥ when results land either way — the inner weather independent of the scoreboard.
verses.connection: The agent-triad opens: passion and freedom proven compatible in one worker.
verses.reflection: Disprove the stereotype in your own person today: blazing zeal, zero clutch — both at once.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: What kind of person does work in the purest way?

views.text: The sattvic agent has given up attachment, does not assert his ego, has fortitude and diligence, and stays unperturbed by success or failure, led only by the authority of the scriptures, not by attachment to results.
Defines the pair: steadiness is persevering in a begun act despite the pain till it is finished; zeal is an active, willing mind.
'Not speaking of I' targets the habitual or intentional claim 'I am the agent'; it does not forbid a yogin from saying 'I do' in ordinary worldly speech.
Anahaṃvādī simply means free of boastful speech; unmoved means without elation or dejection whether the begun act succeeds or fails.
Sattvic doers are not inactive; they work with zeal and resolve but with pure motives, unattached and free of ego, giving God the credit for their success.

verses.devanagari:
रागी कर्मफलप्रेप्सुर्लुब्धो हिंसात्मकोऽशुचिः ।
हर्षशोकान्वितः कर्ता राजसः परिकीर्तितः॥
verses.transliteration:
rāgī karmaphalaprepsurlubdho hiṃsātmako'śuciḥ
harṣaśokānvitaḥ kartā rājasaḥ parikīrtitaḥ
verses.essence: Passionate, hungering for the fruit of action, greedy, violent-natured, impure, swept by joy and sorrow — such an agent is proclaimed rajasic.
verses.translation: Passionate, desiring to obtain the reward of actions, greedy, cruel, impure, moved by joy and sorrow, such an agent is said to be Rajasic (passionate).

anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + फल (fruit) + प्रेप्सु (seeking) — 'one who seeks the fruits of action'
हिंसा (harm) + आत्मक (natured) — 'whose nature is to harm'
अ (not) + शुचि (pure) — 'not pure'
हर्ष (joy) + शोक (grief) + अन्वित (accompanied) — 'accompanied by joy and grief'

verses.explanation: The rajasic doer in six strokes, ending with the signature: harṣa-śokānvitaḥ — *yoked to* elation and grief, riding the result like a small boat rides swells. Every win a high, every setback a wound; the work itself barely tasted between scoreboard checks. Hiṁsātmakaḥ: where wanting is fierce enough, others become obstacles, and obstacles get pushed.
verses.connection: The driven middle: the worker whose mood is outsourced to outcomes.
verses.reflection: Listen for the scoreboard in your mood today — elation and gloom riding results — and step off once.

verses.hook: What drives a person who works out of craving and ambition?

views.text: Greed is wanting others' property and not giving one's own even at holy places; joy and sorrow come as one's actions are aided or hindered.
Reads each mark as a fault in doing the work: 'greedy' is not spending the wealth the act requires, 'impure' is lacking the purity it needs, joy and grief ride victory or defeat.
Rajasic workers chase material gain, believing worldly pleasures satisfy. Never content, they become greedy, envious and sometimes immoral, their lives a mix of elation and dejection.

verses.devanagari:
अयुक्तः प्राकृतः स्तब्धः शठो नैष्कृतिकोऽलसः ।
विषादी दीर्घसूत्री च कर्ता तामस उच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
ayuktaḥ prākṛtaḥ stabdhaḥ śaṭho naiṣkṛtiko'lasaḥ
viṣādī dīrghasūtrī ca kartā tāmasa ucyate
verses.essence: Undisciplined, vulgar, obstinate, deceitful, malicious, lazy, despondent, procrastinating — such an agent is called tamasic.
verses.translation: Unsteady, vulgar, unbending, cheating, malicious, lazy, desponding and procrastinating such an agent is called Tamasic.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + युक्त (steady) — 'not steady'
दीर्घ (long) + सूत्रिन् (with a thread) — 'one who draws the thread out long'

verses.explanation: The tamasic doer's eight marks include the Gita's most domestic word: dīrgha-sūtrī — 'long-threaded', the one whose every task trails endlessly, never cut and tied; and viṣādī, the chronically sunk. Note where viṣāda began: it was Arjuna's own state in chapter 1, this scripture's starting point — named there as a yoga's first step, named here as a strand to outgrow.
verses.connection: The agent-triad closes — 18.29 turns inward again, to the faculties of judgment and resolve.
verses.reflection: Find your longest-threaded task — the one trailing for months — and cut and tie one end today.

verses.hook: What are the traits of a lazy, careless, stubborn worker?

refs.note: The detached worker is sattvic, the attached rajasic, the undiscerning tamasic; one surrendered to God transcends all three modes.

views.text: Gives the marks concretely: stiff like a staff, bowing to no one; hiding his own powers; ruining others' livelihood; not doing in a month what is due today or tomorrow.
Reads the tamasic doer as one engaged in perverse acts like black magic, and 'dilatory' as patiently working long-standing harm on others.
Tamasic workers are undisciplined, closed to reason, cunning and vulgar. Seeing effort as painful, they are lazy and procrastinate, and their base thoughts leave them morose.

verses.devanagari:
बुद्धेर्भेदं धृतेश्चैव गुणतस्त्रिविधं शृणु ।
प्रोच्यमानमशेषेण पृथक्त्वेन धनञ्जय॥
verses.transliteration:
buddherbhedaṃ dhṛteścaiva guṇatastrividhaṃ śṛṇu
procyamānamaśeṣeṇa pṛthaktvena dhanañjaya
verses.essence: Hear now, Dhananjaya, the threefold division of understanding and of steadfastness, according to the gunas — declared completely and severally.
verses.translation: Hear thou the threefold division of intellect and firmness according to the Gunas, as I declare them fully and distinctly, O Arjuna.

anvaya.parts: त्रि (three) + विधा (kind) — 'having three kinds'

anvaya.form: present passive participle, masculine, accusative singular
adjective used as adverb, instrumental singular (fully)
noun, neuter, instrumental singular (by way of)

anvaya.parts: धन (wealth) + जय (winning) — 'he who won wealth'

verses.explanation: Two more instruments under the lens: buddhi, the faculty that *discerns* — tells path from precipice — and dhṛti, the deep grip that *holds* a course once chosen. Compass and keel. A life steers by both, so the field guide must grade both: six more portraits, after which the survey turns to happiness itself.
verses.connection: Announces the buddhi and dhriti triads (18.30–35): how we judge, and how we hold.
verses.reflection: Service both instruments today: the compass that discerns, the keel that holds. A life steers by both.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: Which two inner faculties steer and sustain all our work?

views.text: The threefold classification of intellect and fortitude by the guṇas is stated here in brief, to be given next fully and severally; Arjuna is Dhanañjaya for winning great human and divine wealth in his conquests.
Buddhi is discriminative, determinate knowledge; dhṛti is the resolve to hold on to what one has begun against every obstacle.
Takes dhṛti as contentment: after any act, good or wicked, everyone feels 'what had to be done is done' — this is what lets one withdraw from it.
Intellect and determination propel, control and direct action. Intellect discerns right from wrong, and determination persists despite obstacles; both vary by the three modes.

verses.devanagari:
प्रवृत्तिं च निवृत्तिं च कार्याकार्ये भयाभये ।
बन्धं मोक्षं च या वेत्ति बुद्धिः सा पार्थ सात्त्विकी॥
verses.transliteration:
pravṛttiṃ ca nivṛttiṃ ca kāryākārye bhayābhaye
bandhaṃ mokṣaṃ ca yā vetti buddhiḥ sā pārtha sāttvikī
verses.essence: The understanding that knows action and withdrawal, what ought and ought not be done, fear and fearlessness, bondage and liberation — that, Partha, is sattvic.
verses.translation: The intellect which knows the path of work and renunciation, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fear and fearlessness, bondage and liberation that intellect is Sattvic (pure), O Arjuna.

anvaya.meaning: what should and should not be done
anvaya.parts: कार्य (to be done) + अकार्य (not to be done) — 'duty and non-duty'
भय (fear) + अभय (fearlessness) — 'fear and its absence'

verses.explanation: Sattvic understanding holds four distinctions clean: when to act and when to stand back; what duty asks and forbids; what genuinely merits fear and what doesn't; what binds and what frees. Note the modesty of the claim — not omniscience, just an unclouded compass on the questions that steer a life. Most tragedy flows from confusing exactly these pairs.
verses.connection: The clear compass — precisely the discrimination Arjuna lacked at 1.30 and asked for at 2.7.
verses.reflection: Test the four clean distinctions today: act or refrain, ought or ought-not, fear or no, binds or frees.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: What does a clear, discerning intellect understand?

views.text: Because they stand beside bondage and freedom, pravṛtti and nivṛtti mean the path of works, which binds, and the path of renunciation, which frees; knowing is a function of the intellect, and firmness is another.
Pravṛtti and nivṛtti are the two dharmas, for worldly welfare and for release; fear and fearlessness are traced to transgressing or keeping the scriptures.
Pravṛtti and nivṛtti mean engaging in dharma and turning from adharma, judged by place and time; the intellect 'knows' only figuratively, as one says the firewood cooks.
Our choices shape where we end up, and choosing well needs discrimination. The Gita gave Arjuna this power; a sattvic intellect knows what to do, what to avoid and what to fear.

verses.devanagari:
यया धर्ममधर्मं च कार्यं चाकार्यमेव च ।
अयथावत्प्रजानाति बुद्धिः सा पार्थ राजसी॥
verses.transliteration:
yayā dharmamadharmaṃ ca kāryaṃ cākāryameva ca
ayathāvatprajānāti buddhiḥ sā pārtha rājasī
verses.essence: That by which one knows dharma and adharma, what should and should not be done, incorrectly — that understanding, Partha, is rajasic.
verses.translation: That, by which one wrongly understands Dharma and Adharma and also what ought to be done and what ought not to be done that intellect, O Arjuna, is Rajasic (passionate).

anvaya.form: gerundive (to be done), neuter, accusative singular
gerundive (not to be done), neuter, accusative singular

verses.explanation: The rajasic compass: ayathāvat — *not as it is*; the needle works but reads a few degrees off, deflected by the magnet of self-interest. Right and wrong are perceived, then quietly redrawn around desire: the convenient becomes the correct. Most rationalization lives here — judgment intact enough to be persuasive, bent enough to mislead.
verses.connection: The deflected middle: discernment in service of the wanting self.
verses.reflection: Watch for the deflected needle today — right and wrong quietly redrawn around what you want.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: Why do even capable people misjudge right and wrong?

views.text: Ayathāvat means not discerning from every side: dharma and adharma refer to the scriptures' seen and unseen results, kārya and akārya to actually doing or not doing.
'Wrongly' here means in a state of doubt: the rajasic intellect is left uncertain rather than flatly reversed.
The rajasic intellect sees clearly until self-interest enters, then blurs. Attachments leave it confused between important and trivial, lasting and passing.

verses.devanagari:
अधर्मं धर्ममिति या मन्यते तमसावृता ।
सर्वार्थान्विपरीतांश्च बुद्धिः सा पार्थ तामसी॥
verses.transliteration:
adharmaṃ dharmamiti yā manyate tamasāvṛtā
sarvārthānviparītāṃśca buddhiḥ sā pārtha tāmasī
verses.essence: That which, enveloped in darkness, regards adharma as dharma and sees all things reversed — that understanding, Partha, is tamasic.
verses.translation: That, which, enveloped in darkness, sees Adharma as Dharma and all things perverted that intellect, O Arjuna, is Tamasic (dark).

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + अर्थ (thing) — 'all things'

verses.explanation: The broken compass: not deflected but inverted — adharmaṁ dharmam iti, wrong worn confidently as right, sarvārthān viparītān, the whole map upside down. The fearful trait of tamasic judgment is its certainty: rajas suspects its own bending; tamas marches, convinced, in precisely the wrong direction. History's catastrophes are mostly this verse at scale.
verses.connection: The inverted compass completes the buddhi-triad; 18.33 turns to what holds a course.
verses.reflection: Beware certainty traveling in exactly the wrong direction — check one conviction's compass today.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: What happens when the mind sees wrong as right?

views.text: The tamasic intellect, covered by darkness, takes vice, what is prohibited, for virtue, what is prescribed, and perceives all objects of knowledge without exception as contrary to what they are.
Spells out 'reversed': dharma as adharma and back, the existent as non-existent, higher truth as lower — every value turned over.
Adds a note on terms: buddhi is the inner organ, while knowledge and firmness are its functions; these three are singled out because they serve dharma and adharma.
Lacking the light of knowledge, the tamasic intellect mistakes adharma for dharma, like a drunk blind to his own ruin, and loses judgment and reasoning.

verses.devanagari:
धृत्या यया धारयते मनःप्राणेन्द्रियक्रियाः ।
योगेनाव्यभिचारिण्या धृतिः सा पार्थ सात्त्विकी॥
verses.transliteration:
dhṛtyā yayā dhārayate manaḥprāṇendriyakriyāḥ
yogenāvyabhicāriṇyā dhṛtiḥ sā pārtha sāttvikī
verses.essence: The steadfastness by which one holds the activities of mind, breath and senses through unswerving yoga — that steadfastness, Partha, is sattvic.
verses.translation: The unwavering firmness by which, through Yoga, the functions of the mind, the life-force and the senses are restrained that firmness, O Arjuna, is Sattvic (pure).

anvaya.meaning: activities of mind, breath and senses
anvaya.parts: मनस् (mind) + प्राण (breath) + इन्द्रिय (sense) + क्रिया (activity) — 'the workings of mind, breath and senses'

anvaya.form: adjective, feminine, instrumental singular (agrees with 'by firmness')
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + व्यभिचारिन् (straying) — 'never straying'

verses.explanation: Sattvic dhṛti: the keel — a steadiness that holds the whole apparatus, thought, breath and sense, on one heading, avyabhicāriṇyā, without straying. This is the grip that survives dull Tuesdays and broken moods, the force behind every practice still alive after twenty years. Not intensity: constancy — the rarer and stronger of the two.
verses.connection: The holding-power triad opens: resolve in service of the undivided aim.
verses.reflection: Hold one heading all day — thought, breath, and senses on a single course — and call it dhriti.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: What kind of determination holds mind, breath and senses steady?

views.text: Firmness is unfailing because it is ever joined with samādhi; with it one keeps mind, breath and senses from moving toward what the scriptures forbid.
Yoga here is worship of the Lord as the means of release; sattvic firmness sustains the organs in that worship until the goal is reached.
Mere willpower cannot hold mind and senses; firmness must be joined with concentration. It is not repression but intelligent sublimation and inner transformation.
Determination is the inner strength to persevere toward the goal. Sattvic determination grows through yoga, as one learns to subdue the senses, discipline the breath and control the mind.

verses.devanagari:
यया तु धर्मकामार्थान्धृत्या धारयतेऽर्जुन ।
प्रसङ्गेन फलाकाङ्क्षी धृतिः सा पार्थ राजसी॥
verses.transliteration:
yayā tu dharmakāmārthāndhṛtyā dhārayate'rjuna
prasaṅgena phalākāṅkṣī dhṛtiḥ sā pārtha rājasī
verses.essence: But the steadfastness by which one holds to duty, pleasure and wealth, craving the fruits of each as occasion offers — that steadfastness, Partha, is rajasic.
verses.translation: But that, O Arjuna, by which, on account of attachment and desire for reward, one holds fast to Dharma (duty), enjoyment of pleasures and earning of wealth that firmness, O Arjuna, is Rajasic (passionate).

anvaya.base: धर्म · duty; काम · desire; अर्थ · wealth
anvaya.parts: धर्म (duty) + काम (pleasure) + अर्थ (wealth) — the three worldly aims
फल (fruit) + आकाङ्क्षिन् (longing) — 'one who longs for results'

verses.explanation: Rajasic dhṛti is genuinely strong — it powers careers, fortunes, reputations — but its grip serves the three worldly aims with phalākāṅkṣī stamped on each: holding *in order to harvest*. Such steadiness lasts exactly as long as the returns do; the project that stops paying gets dropped, however worthy. Tenacity on commission.
verses.connection: The transactional grip: strong hands, hired by results.
verses.reflection: Notice which commitments you keep only while they pay — tenacity on commission.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas.
