verses.hook: What kind of determination is driven by wanting the rewards?

views.text: Takes prasaṅgena as 'as each occasion arises': one is convinced the three aims must always be pursued and grows desirous of the fruit of whichever is at hand.
Takes prasaṅgena as intense attachment; the three aims stand for the activities of mind, breath and senses kept up as means to duty, pleasure and wealth.
Worldly people can be just as determined as yogis, but their resolve is fuelled by the wish to enjoy results, so they cling to money as the means to pleasure; such determination belongs to passion.

verses.devanagari:
यया स्वप्नं भयं शोकं विषादं मदमेव च ।
न विमुञ्चति दुर्मेधा धृतिः सा पार्थ तामसी॥
verses.transliteration:
yayā svapnaṃ bhayaṃ śokaṃ viṣādaṃ madameva ca
na vimuñcati durmedhā dhṛtiḥ sā pārtha tāmasī
verses.essence: That by which a dull person does not let go of sleep, fear, grief, despondency and conceit — that steadfastness, Partha, is tamasic.
verses.translation: That, by which a stupid man does not abandon sleep, fear, grief, despair and also conceit that firmness, O Arjuna, is Tamasic.

anvaya.parts: दुर् (bad) + मेधा (intelligence) — 'one whose understanding is corrupt'

verses.explanation: The triad's darkest insight: tamas also has a grip — and it is iron. Na vimuñcati, *does not let go*: of oversleep, of fear long after the danger, of grief turned residence, of viṣāda, of self-flattering illusion. The same holding-power that could anchor a practice instead anchors the misery. Tenacity, the verse teaches, is neutral; everything depends on what the fist is closed around.
verses.connection: Completes dhriti: even despair requires a kind of strength — misapplied.
verses.reflection: Find where your strength grips the wrong cargo — fear kept, grief kept, gloom kept — and open one fist.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: What does stubbornness rooted in fear, grief and pride look like?

views.text: Mada is sensual enjoyment; the dull man holds these as always to be resorted to and greatly important, like a drunkard thinking of wine.
Tamasic contentment fixes its pleasure only in things like sleep and fighting.
'Does not let go' means he brings them back again and again; svapna here means sleep.
Dull people also show tenacity, but it is the obstinate clinging to fear, old disappointments and wounded pride, even when it ruins them; that is determination in the mode of ignorance.

verses.devanagari:
सुखं त्विदानीं त्रिविधं शृणु मे भरतर्षभ ।
अभ्यासाद्रमते यत्र दुःखान्तं च निगच्छति॥
verses.transliteration:
sukhaṃ tvidānīṃ trividhaṃ śṛṇu me bharatarṣabha
abhyāsādramate yatra duḥkhāntaṃ ca nigacchati
verses.essence: And now hear from me, bull of the Bharatas, the threefold happiness: that in which one comes to delight through practice, and reaches the end of sorrow —
verses.translation: And now hear from Me, O Arjuna, of the threefold pleasure, in which one rejoices by practice and surely comes to the end of pain.

anvaya.parts: त्रि (three) + विधा (kind) — 'having three kinds'
भरत (Bharata's line) + ऋषभ (bull) — 'best of the Bharatas'
दुःख (sorrow) + अन्त (end) — 'the end of suffering'

verses.explanation: The survey's final and most intimate subject: sukha, happiness itself — for every strand sells its own brand, and choosing among them is the whole art of a life. The sattvic kind is introduced by two credentials: abhyāsāt ramate, it must be *practiced into* — no instant delivery — and it actually ends sorrow rather than postponing it.
verses.connection: Opens the happiness-triad (18.36–39): the deepest diagnostic of all — what does your joy cost, and when?
verses.reflection: Ask of today's happiness the master question: what does this joy cost, and when is the bill due?
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. verses.hook: What kinds of happiness are there, and which one ends sorrow?

views.text: The threefold joy is that in which one delights through habit, by frequent repetition, and in the experience of which one certainly reaches the cessation of sorrow.
Happiness is the end to which knowledge, action and agent are all subservient; through long practice one reaches incomparable joy and is not again engulfed by saṃsāra.
Unlike sense pleasure, which delights at once, this joy is reached through long familiarity; the second line already begins the description of sattvic happiness.
Every action is ultimately a search for happiness, and because people's actions differ in their makeup, the happiness they find differs too; Krishna now sorts it into three kinds.

verses.devanagari:
यत्तदग्रे विषमिव परिणामेऽमृतोपमम् ।
तत्सुखं सात्त्विकं प्रोक्तमात्मबुद्धिप्रसादजम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yattadagre viṣamiva pariṇāme'mṛtopamam
tatsukhaṃ sāttvikaṃ proktamātmabuddhiprasādajam
verses.essence: — that which is like poison at first but like nectar in the end, born of the serene clarity of self-understanding: that happiness is declared sattvic.
verses.translation: That which is like poison at first but in the end like nectar that happiness is declared to be Sattvic, born of the purity of one's own mind due to Self-realisation.

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, locative singular (at), used as an adverb

anvaya.meaning: in the end, as it ripens

anvaya.parts: अमृत (nectar) + उपम (like): 'having nectar as its likeness'

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter nominative singular (is said)

anvaya.meaning: born of the clarity of self-directed understanding
anvaya.base: आत्मन् + बुद्धि + प्रसाद + ज · self + intellect + clarity + born
anvaya.parts: आत्म (self) + बुद्धि (understanding) + प्रसाद (clearness, serenity) + ज (born): 'born from the clearness of the understanding concerning the self'

verses.explanation: The signature of real happiness: agre viṣam iva — poison first. The early morning practice, the honest conversation, the discipline's first cold weeks: all bitter at the threshold, amṛtopamam — nectar — in the ripening. Its source is given precisely: ātma-buddhi-prasāda-jam, born of the clearing of the understanding as it settles on the self — joy as clarity's by-product, not stimulation's. The verse hands us a test for any joy on offer: plot its curve. Whatever charges admission in discomfort and pays in clarity is sattvic; the reverse curve (18.38) is the world's usual merchandise.
verses.connection: The first taste-curve: bitter-then-sweet — the exact inverse of what 18.38 describes.
verses.reflection: Choose one poison-first pleasure today — the practice, the honest talk — and trust the nectar at the end.

Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: Which happiness tastes bitter at first but sweet in the end?

refs.note: Distinguishes the beneficial from the pleasant: the pleasant charms at first but ends in pain, while the wise choose the beneficial and reach real happiness, matching sattvic joy.

views.text: The early bitterness is the hard struggle of acquiring knowledge, detachment, meditation and absorption; the nectar comes as these mature. Prasāda is the water-like clearness of the intellect, or the high clarity of knowledge of the Self.

It tastes like poison at the start of yoga because effort is strenuous and the self's own nature is not yet experienced; once the understanding is withdrawn from all objects and turned to the self, its joy becomes elixir.

It is poison at first because attachment to sense-objects, built up over hundreds of lives, is extremely hard to give up; the serenity of mind follows from serenity in the Self, where nothing else remains to be sought.
Compares it to a bitter medicine like nux vomica: yama, niyama, austerity, sense-control and early meditation hurt, but the cured aspirant finally rejoices in the Self.
Like the bitter gooseberry that soon turns sweet and heals, sattvic happiness is hard at the start but nectar later; it is the beneficial path the Vedas set against the merely pleasant.

verses.devanagari:
विषयेन्द्रियसंयोगाद्यत्तदग्रेऽमृतोपमम् ।
परिणामे विषमिव तत्सुखं राजसं स्मृतम्॥
verses.transliteration:
viṣayendriyasaṃyogādyattadagre'mṛtopamam
pariṇāme viṣamiva tatsukhaṃ rājasaṃ smṛtam
verses.essence: That which arises from the contact of senses with their objects — like nectar at first but like poison in the end: that happiness is held to be rajasic.
verses.translation: That happiness which arises from the contact of the sense-organs with the objects, which is at first like nectar, and in the end like poison that is declared to be Rajasic.

anvaya.meaning: from contact of senses with objects
anvaya.base: विषय + इन्द्रिय + संयोग · object + sense + union
anvaya.parts: विषय (sense-object) + इन्द्रिय (sense-organ) + संयोग (contact): 'from the contact of the senses and their objects'

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, locative singular (at), used as an adverb

anvaya.parts: अमृत (nectar) + उपम (like): 'having nectar as its likeness'

anvaya.meaning: in the end, as it ripens

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter nominative singular (is held to be)

verses.explanation: The same curve, reversed: nectar at the first sip, poison in the sediment — the indulgence, the conquest, the thrill, each sweet exactly while the senses touch their object and souring as the contact fades into craving, depletion, consequence. Neither curve is moralized; they are simply *plotted*, and the reader is left holding the graph of their own evenings.
verses.connection: The mirrored taste-curve: pleasure that invoices later — most of what the market calls happiness.
verses.reflection: Watch one nectar-first pleasure turn today — sweet at contact, souring in the sediment — just watch.
verses.background: The great threefold catalogue unrolls — the chapter's longest movement: knowledge that sees the one imperishable in all beings, or only separateness, or one fragment as the whole; action obligatory and unattached, or strained by desire, or undertaken blindly; the doer free of ego, or greedy and volatile, or indolent and despairing; then intellect, firmness, and finally happiness itself — poison first and nectar after for sattva, nectar first and poison after for rajas, delusion throughout for tamas. Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: Why does pleasure that starts sweet so often end in pain?

views.text: The poison at the end is concrete: full enjoyment drains strength, vigour, beauty, understanding, memory, wealth and diligence, and becomes a cause of wrongdoing and its consequences.
Places the turn precisely: nectar while the senses meet agreeable objects, poison when satiety sets in or over-indulgence leaves one unable to enjoy any more.
A grain of sensual pleasure comes with a mountain of pain: fear of losing the object, attachment, the wrongdoing done to get money, and senses and intellect dulled by indulgence.
Rajasic joy is a thrill born of sense contact that lasts only as long as the contact, leaving greed, anxiety and guilt behind; lasting bliss comes through discipline and renunciation, not indulgence.

verses.devanagari:
यदग्रे चानुबन्धे च सुखं मोहनमात्मनः ।
निद्रालस्यप्रमादोत्थं तत्तामसमुदाहृतम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yadagre cānubandhe ca sukhaṃ mohanamātmanaḥ
nidrālasyapramādotthaṃ tattāmasamudāhṛtam
verses.essence: That happiness which deludes the self both at the start and in the sequel — arising from sleep, sloth and heedlessness — is declared tamasic.
verses.translation: That happiness which at first as well as in the sequel deludes the self, and which arises from sleep, indolence and heedlessness that is declared to be Tamasic.

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, locative singular (at), used as an adverb

verses.explanation: The third curve never rises: mohanam ātmanaḥ at both ends — a comfort that fogs going in and fogs coming out. The oversleep, the numbing scroll, the haze chosen *because* it is haze: not pleasure exactly, but anesthesia mistaken for rest. Its three springs — sleep beyond need, sloth, heedlessness — are tamas's own roster from 14.8, now sold as happiness.
verses.connection: The flat-line comfort completes the triad; 18.40 closes the whole survey with a universal law.
verses.reflection: Name the flat-line comfort honestly once: the haze chosen because it is haze. Anesthesia is not rest.

Nothing on earth or in heaven is free of the three strands.
verses.hook: What happiness deludes you from beginning to end?

views.text: Tamasic joy deludes oneself both at the beginning and after the enjoyment ends, and arises from sleep, laziness and inadvertence; the next verse concludes this section.
Delusion means not knowing things as they are. Sloth slows the senses and heedlessness neglects duty, so both dim knowledge; the lesson is to subdue rajas and tamas and let sattva alone grow.
Takes pramāda as inattention to what must be done, which breeds idle daydreaming; the 'pleasure' of tamas rises from sleep, sloth and that drifting reverie.
Anubandha is the after-effect. The pleasures of bad habits such as drinking or eating worthless food delude a person until he forgets the path he ought to walk.
Tamasic pleasure is folly throughout and darkens the soul, yet its small taste of pleasure makes it addictive, as with smokers who cannot quit though they know it harms them.

verses.devanagari:
न तदस्ति पृथिव्यां वा दिवि देवेषु वा पुनः ।
सत्त्वं प्रकृतिजैर्मुक्तं यदेभिः स्यात्त्रिभिर्गुणैः॥
verses.transliteration:
na tadasti pṛthivyāṃ vā divi deveṣu vā punaḥ
sattvaṃ prakṛtijairmuktaṃ yadebhiḥ syāttribhirguṇaiḥ
verses.essence: There is no being, whether on earth or again among the gods in heaven, that is free from these three gunas born of prakriti.
verses.translation: There is no being on earth or again in heaven among the gods, that is liberated from the three qualities born of Nature.

anvaya.parts: प्रकृति (nature, matter) + ज (born): 'born of prakriti'

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter nominative singular

verses.explanation: The survey seals itself with a totality clause: nothing anywhere — no creature, no king, no *god* — stands outside the three strands; the whole ladder of existence, bottom to shining top, is woven of them. The field guide is therefore universal, and so is its implication: within nature there is no exit, only better weather. The exit lies elsewhere — and the chapter now turns to find it through one's own born work.
verses.connection: Closes the guna-survey absolutely — pivoting to 18.41: if no one escapes the strands, each must work through their own.
verses.reflection: Stop waiting for strand-free people today — no one born of nature is. Seek better weather in yourself instead.

verses.hook: Is any being, human or divine, free of nature's three qualities?

refs.note: Describes material nature as three-coloured, white, red and black, the womb of countless beings; the soul that enjoys her is bound, showing all creatures fall under the three modes.

views.text: Raises the problem this creates: if everything is made of the gunas, how can the root of worldly existence be cut? The verses on each class's duties begin in order to answer that and to sum up the Gita.
From Brahmā down to immobile things, nothing rooted in prakṛti escapes the gunas; the whole threefold analysis was given so that the seeker would know sattva is what must be cultivated.
From Brahmā to the worm no one is truly happy, since all stay bound to the triad of strands; real happiness belongs only to the one whose mind has gone beyond them.
The gunas are the warp and woof of everything, as threads are of cloth; only the liberated sage who knows the Self stops the wheel they turn.
Maya is made of the three modes, so every realm from the lowest to Brahma's abode is under them; beings differ only in their proportions, which is why human natures differ.

verses.devanagari:
ब्राह्मणक्षत्रियविशां शूद्राणां च परन्तप ।
कर्माणि प्रविभक्तानि स्वभावप्रभवैर्गुणैः॥
verses.transliteration:
brāhmaṇakṣatriyaviśāṃ śūdrāṇāṃ ca parantapa
karmāṇi pravibhaktāni svabhāvaprabhavairguṇaiḥ
verses.essence: The duties of brahmanas, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras, Parantapa, are distributed according to the qualities born of their own natures.
verses.translation: Of Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and Vaisyas, as also of Sudras, O Arjuna, the duties are distributed according to the qualities born of their own nature.

anvaya.base: ब्राह्मण + क्षत्रिय + विश् · priest + warrior + farmer-trader
anvaya.parts: ब्राह्मण (brahmana) + क्षत्रिय (kshatriya) + विश् (vaishya): a list compound, 'of the three'

anvaya.base: शूद्र · member of the serving class

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter nominative plural (are divided)

anvaya.parts: स्व (own) + भाव (being) + प्रभव (origin): 'which spring from one's own nature'

verses.explanation: The chapter turns from analysis to vocation, and its stated basis matters: svabhāva-prabhavaiḥ guṇaiḥ — work apportioned by the *qualities arising from one's own nature*, the guna-composition just surveyed in 18.19–40. The verse itself names guṇa and svabhāva, not birth; the classical commentators trace that nature to past karma and the birth it shapes, while modern readers stress temperament. Either way, the question it asks of a person is what their nature is made of, and what work that nature can pour itself into.
verses.connection: Applies the completed guna-science to vocation — read with 4.13, where the same division is tied to guna and karma.
verses.reflection: Read your own composition today — what qualities actually arise from your nature — and assign work accordingly.
verses.background: The teaching turns to vocation: the works of brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya, and shudra are apportioned by the qualities born of inner nature — serenity and knowledge; heroism and lordly generosity; agriculture, cattle, trade; and service. Devoted each to his own work, a person attains perfection — worshiping, through his own duty, Him from whom all beings arise. Better one's own dharma though flawed; the work born with you, though faulty, should not be abandoned, for all undertakings are veiled by fault as fire by smoke.
verses.hook: On what basis were the four kinds of social duty divided?

views.text: Offers two readings of svabhāva: God's prakṛti made of the three gunas, or the tendencies earned in past lives now ripening. Brahmanas are marked by sattva, kshatriyas by rajas with sattva, vaishyas by rajas with tamas, shudras by tamas with rajas.
Past karma determines birth into a class, the gunas follow from that karma, and the śāstras then allot duties to match those dispositions.
Opens a new section that gathers the whole Gita: since everything is threefold, liberation comes by worshipping the Lord through one's prescribed work and gaining knowledge by His grace.
The original varna system assigned work according to each person's nature and qualities, not birth or rank; it later decayed into a rigid birth-based caste order, which was never its intent.

verses.devanagari:
शमो दमस्तपः शौचं क्षान्तिरार्जवमेव च ।
ज्ञानं विज्ञानमास्तिक्यं ब्रह्मकर्म स्वभावजम्॥

śamo damastapaḥ śaucaṃ kṣāntirārjavameva ca
jñānaṃ vijñānamāstikyaṃ brahmakarma svabhāvajam

verses.translation: Serenity, self-restraint, austerity, purity, forgiveness and also uprightness, knowledge, realisation and belief in God are the duties of the Brahmanas, born of (their own) nature.

verses.explanation: The contemplative nature described by its outputs: inner calm and outer restraint, the scrubbed life, patience, straightness, learning ripened into vijñāna — lived realization — and āstikya, the settled trust that reality has a depth. Note that everything listed is a quality, not a privilege: this 'work' is a way of being that teaches by existing.
verses.connection: First of the four nature-portraits (18.42–44): the temperament whose work is clarity itself.
verses.reflection: Borrow one brahmana-quality for the day: calm, restraint, or the settled trust that reality has depth.

views.text: Śama is control of the inner organ, dama of the outer senses; āstikya is conviction in the truth of scripture's teaching. 'Born of nature' repeats the point of the previous verse: classified by the gunas.

Reverses the pair (śama outer senses, dama mind) and gives āstikya full content: unshakable conviction that Vāsudeva is the Supreme Brahman, cause and support of all, worshipped through every Vedic act.
Separates the two knowledges: jñāna is what the scriptures teach, vijñāna is direct experience; āstikya is the settled certainty that a world beyond this one exists.

Those with predominantly sattvic natures were Brahmins: given to austerity, purity, devotion and learning, they taught, performed rituals and advised rulers by their wisdom rather than governing themselves.

verses.devanagari:
शौर्यं तेजो धृतिर्दाक्ष्यं युद्धे चाप्यपलायनम् ।
दानमीश्वरभावश्च क्षात्रं कर्म स्वभावजम्॥

śauryaṃ tejo dhṛtirdākṣyaṃ yuddhe cāpyapalāyanam
dānamīśvarabhāvaśca kṣātraṃ karma svabhāvajam
verses.essence: Heroism, fire, fortitude, skill, refusal to flee in battle, generosity and lordliness — these are the works of a kshatriya, born of inner nature.
verses.translation: Prowess, splendour, firmness, dexterity and also not fleeing from battle, generosity and lordliness are the duties of the Kshatriyas, born of (their own) nature.

ईश्वर (ruler) + भाव (nature, bearing): 'the bearing of a ruler'

verses.explanation: The guardian nature: courage with tejas behind it, the grip of dhṛti, dākṣya — competence under pressure — and the mark Arjuna cannot miss hearing: yuddhe cāpy apalāyanam, *not fleeing in battle*. Paired, crucially, with dāna and īśvara-bhāva: power that protects and gives, or it is not this dharma at all. The portrait is a mirror held up to the listener.
verses.connection: Arjuna's own nature read back to him — the verse beneath Krishna's entire case since 2.31.
verses.reflection: Borrow one kshatriya-quality too: stand somewhere today where retreating would be easier.

verses.hook: What qualities mark the nature and work of a warrior?

views.text: Dhṛti is not sinking under any circumstance; dākṣya is acting without confusion when duties arrive suddenly; īśvarabhāva is exercising rule over those who are to be ruled.
Raises each quality to its limit: apalāyana is not fleeing even when sure of death, dāna is giving away one's possessions even entirely, tejas is the power to remain undefeated.
Like the sunflower that always faces the sun, the kshatriya always faces his enemies; like a tree giving its fruit, he gives whatever is asked.
Kshatriyas were mainly rajasic with some sattva, which made them heroic, commanding and generous; they governed the land, yet humbly sought the Brahmins' counsel on spiritual and policy matters.

verses.devanagari:
कृषिगौरक्ष्यवाणिज्यं वैश्यकर्म स्वभावजम् ।
परिचर्यात्मकं कर्म शूद्रस्यापि स्वभावजम्॥

kṛṣigaurakṣyavāṇijyaṃ vaiśyakarma svabhāvajam
paricaryātmakaṃ karma śūdrasyāpi svabhāvajam

verses.translation: Agriculture, cattle-rearing and trade are the duties of the Vaisya (merchant), born of (their own) nature; and action consisting of service is the duty of the Sudra (servant-class), born of (their own) nature.

verses.explanation: The remaining two portraits: the productive nature — growing, tending, trading, the arts that feed and circulate a world — and the nature whose gift is paricaryā, direct service and support. The refrain svabhāvajam sounds a fourth time, insisting on its frame: these are descriptions of temperament finding its channel. And the verses that follow immediately level the field — what matters is not *which* work, but what one does with one's own.
verses.connection: Completes the four portraits — so that 18.45–46 can declare them equal at the summit.
verses.reflection: Honor the producers and the servers in your world today — feeding and supporting are sacred grammar.

verses.hook: What work suits the merchant and the worker by nature?

views.text: Duties of the classes, rightly done, by themselves bring heaven and a better birth, as the Dharma-sūtras say; the higher result about to be named comes from a different cause.

These occupations are auxiliary to the sacrifices the śāstra ordains. Sense-control is named as the brahmana's duty because his sattva makes it natural for him, while rajas and tamas make it hard for the others.
Vaishyas, rajasic with some tamas, built wealth through trade and farming, sustained the economy and gave in charity; Shudras progressed best by serving society as artisans, craftsmen and workers.

स्वे स्वे कर्मण्यभिरतः संसिद्धिं लभते नरः ।
स्वकर्मनिरतः सिद्धिं यथा विन्दति तच्छृणु॥

sve sve karmaṇyabhirataḥ saṃsiddhiṃ labhate naraḥ
svakarmanirataḥ siddhiṃ yathā vindati tacchṛṇu

verses.translation: Each person devoted to their own duty attains perfection. How they attain perfection while being engaged in their own duty, hear now.

Not perfection despite one's station but through it; the door is wherever you are standing. Abhirataḥ, *delighting* in it: the Gita asks not for resignation to one's work but for a wholeheartedness that turns the work transparent.
verses.connection: Universalizes the four portraits: every authentic vocation reaches the same summit — 18.46 gives the mechanism.
verses.reflection: Delight in your own work once today — abhirata — perfection enters through the door you already stand at.

views.text: One's own duty, carried out wholeheartedly as dedication to the Lord and without expecting fruits, washes the mind clean and makes one fit for Self-knowledge. Work alone does not give liberation; it prepares the heart for it.
Doing the duties that fit our nature uses body and mind constructively, purifying us and benefiting society; as our competence grows, our duty rises too, and we keep advancing.

verses.devanagari:
यतः प्रवृत्तिर्भूतानां येन सर्वमिदं ततम् ।
स्वकर्मणा तमभ्यर्च्य सिद्धिं विन्दति मानवः॥
verses.transliteration:
yataḥ pravṛttirbhūtānāṃ yena sarvamidaṃ tatam
svakarmaṇā tamabhyarcya siddhiṃ vindati mānavaḥ
verses.essence: Worshiping, through one's own work, the One from whom all beings arise and by whom all this is pervaded — a person finds perfection.
verses.translation: He from Whom all the beings have evolved and by Whom all this is pervaded worshipping Him with his own duty, man attains perfection.

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter, nominative singular

anvaya.parts: स्व (own) + कर्म (work): 'one's own work'

verses.explanation: The mechanism, and one of the Gita's supreme verses: sva-karmaṇā tam abhyarcya — worship Him *with your own work*. The deed itself becomes the offering: the field ploughed, the ledger kept, the patient tended, the line of code — each laid before the One from whom beings arise and by whom all this is pervaded. No change of occupation required, only of address. The commentators differ on the prize: for Śaṅkara the siddhi is fitness for steadfastness in knowledge; for Rāmānuja it is reaching the Lord by His grace. Either way, siddhiṁ vindati mānavaḥ — perfection is found not beside one's livelihood but through it.
verses.connection: The summit of the vocation-teaching: karma-yoga and bhakti fused into a single gesture.
verses.reflection: Make your livelihood the liturgy once today: offer the actual task, as worship, to the All-Pervading.

verses.hook: How can ordinary daily work become a form of worship?

refs.note: A proud ascetic is humbled by a devoted housewife and taught by a righteous butcher that duty done without selfish desire purifies, showing any work offered rightly is worship.

views.text: The siddhi won here is only the fitness for steadfastness in knowledge, not liberation itself; pravṛtti can also mean the activity of creatures, which comes from God as the inner Ruler.
The one worshipped is Krishna himself, abiding as Inner Ruler even in Indra and the gods; the perfection is attaining Him by His grace.
Doing one's own duty carries out the Lord's intention; worshipped with the flowers of one's action, He grants dispassion and discrimination, making one fit for the path of knowledge.
No duty is impure; the consciousness behind it gives it worth. Doing one's own work in devotion joins God's plan for our purification and turns work itself into worship.

verses.translation: Better is one's own duty (though) destitute of merits, than the duty of another well performed. He who does the duty ordained by his own nature incurs no sin.

पर (another) + धर्म (duty): 'another's duty'

anvaya.form: past participle compound, masculine, ablative singular (than)
anvaya.parts: सु (well) + अनुष्ठित (performed): 'well carried out'
स्वभाव (own nature) + नियत (ordained): 'ordained by one's nature'

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while doing)

verses.explanation: The maxim of 3.35 returns for the summation, with its ground now visible: svabhāva-niyatam — the work *your nature itself assigns*. Borrowed callings, however gleaming, run against the grain of what you are; your own, even viguṇa — rough, flawed, unglamorous — runs with it, and so purifies rather than stains. Authenticity outranks polish; the fault lies not in imperfect work but in abandoned selfhood.
verses.connection: 3.35 restated at the summit — now backed by the full svabhava-doctrine of 18.41–46.
verses.reflection: Choose your rough-grained calling over a borrowed gleaming one, again, today — and incur no stain.
verses.background: The teaching turns to vocation: the works of brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya, and shudra are apportioned by the qualities born of inner nature — serenity and knowledge; heroism and lordly generosity; agriculture, cattle, trade; and service. Devoted each to his own work, a person attains perfection — worshiping, through his own duty, Him from whom all beings arise. Better one's own dharma though flawed; the work born with you, though faulty, should not be abandoned, for all undertakings are veiled by fault as fire by smoke.
verses.hook: Is it better to do your own duty poorly than another's well?

refs.note: One should keep doing prescribed duties until a taste for hearing and chanting about God has arisen, supporting the counsel not to abandon one's own work prematurely.

views.text: As a worm born in poison is not harmed by it, one who does the work his own nature dictates incurs no sin.

Reads svadharma as karma-yoga, natural and easy for an embodied person, and 'another's dharma' as jñāna-yoga, which even when done well is always liable to lapses; karma-yoga is better even with flaws.
Applies it to Arjuna directly: do not think a mendicant's life is better than one's own duty of battle, even though battle involves killing kinsmen.
One's own duty fits one's nature, so it flows easily and leaves the mind free for devotion; abandoning it for another's fights one's nature, as Arjun's flight to the forest would.

verses.devanagari:
सहजं कर्म कौन्तेय सदोषमपि न त्यजेत् ।
सर्वारम्भा हि दोषेण धूमेनाग्निरिवावृताः॥
verses.transliteration:
sahajaṃ karma kaunteya sadoṣamapi na tyajet
sarvārambhā hi doṣeṇa dhūmenāgnirivāvṛtāḥ
verses.essence: One should not abandon the work born of one's nature, Kaunteya, though it carry a flaw — for all undertakings are veiled by some fault, as fire by smoke.
verses.translation: One should not abandon, O Arjuna, the duty to which one is born, though faulty; for, all undertakings are enveloped by evil, as fire by smoke.

anvaya.parts: सह (with) + ज (born): 'born along with one'
स (with) + दोष (defect): 'faulty'
सर्व (all) + आरम्भ (undertaking): 'all enterprises'

anvaya.form: past passive participle, masculine, nominative plural

verses.explanation: The verse that disarms perfectionism: sarvārambhā hi doṣeṇa — *every* undertaking, without exception, comes wrapped in some flaw, dhūmenāgnir iva, as fire comes wrapped in smoke. Waiting for stainless work is waiting for smokeless fire. The instruction: keep the sahaja karma, the work you were born carrying, even sadoṣam, with its faults, and let it burn. The smoke is not evidence against the fire — and another's work, looked at closely, smokes too.
verses.connection: Answers the purist's last objection — and frees Arjuna from demanding a war without smoke.
verses.reflection: Expect smoke with every fire today — keep the born work, flaws included; smokeless fire does not exist.
verses.background: The teaching turns to vocation: the works of brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya, and shudra are apportioned by the qualities born of inner nature — serenity and knowledge; heroism and lordly generosity; agriculture, cattle, trade; and service. Devoted each to his own work, a person attains perfection — worshiping, through his own duty, Him from whom all beings arise. Better one's own dharma though flawed; the work born with you, though faulty, should not be abandoned, for all undertakings are veiled by fault as fire by smoke.
verses.hook: Should you quit your work because it has some flaw?

views.text: Born work is faulty because it is made of the three gunas; since an unenlightened person cannot give up action completely, he should not abandon the duty he is born to.
Even one fit for jñāna-yoga should practise karma-yoga: both carry imperfections like smoke, but karma-yoga is easy and not liable to negligence.
As fire is used for its heat while its smoke is set aside, work is pursued for its good part, the purification of sattva, while its faulty part is left.
No work is free of defect, just as fire carries smoke, but one's natural duty offers a comfortable path to purification whose benefits far outweigh its faults, if done in the right consciousness.

verses.devanagari:
असक्तबुद्धिः सर्वत्र जितात्मा विगतस्पृहः ।
नैष्कर्म्यसिद्धिं परमां संन्यासेनाधिगच्छति॥
verses.transliteration:
asaktabuddhiḥ sarvatra jitātmā vigataspṛhaḥ
naiṣkarmyasiddhiṃ paramāṃ saṃnyāsenādhigacchati
verses.essence: With understanding unattached everywhere, self conquered, longing departed — by renunciation one attains the supreme perfection of freedom from action.
verses.translation: He whose intellect is unattached everywhere, who has subdued his self, from whom desire has fled, he by renunciation, attains the supreme state of freedom from action.

anvaya.parts: अ-सक्त (not clinging) + बुद्धि (understanding): 'one whose understanding clings to nothing'
जित (conquered, from √जि) + आत्मा (self): 'one who has mastered himself'
विगत (gone away) + स्पृहा (craving): 'one from whom desire has departed'
नैष्कर्म्य (freedom from action) + सिद्धि (perfection): 'the perfection that is actionlessness'

anvaya.base: संन्यास · renunciation (सम् + नि + √अस् · to lay down)

verses.explanation: The paradoxical prize: naiṣkarmya-siddhi, the perfection of *non-action*. Read with Rāmānuja and Śrīdhara, it is won not by stopping work but by the saṁnyāsa that empties it of clutching: intellect unhooked, self governed, spṛhā gone. One still acts; nothing any longer *acts back* upon one — stillness achieved at full speed. Śaṅkara reads it more starkly: the knower's renunciation of all action, once the actionless Self is known as one's own.
verses.connection: Names the goal of 18.45–48's path — and 18.50 begins describing the final ascent to Brahman.
verses.reflection: Taste actionlessness at full speed once: act completely, with nothing in you grasping the act.
verses.background: The final ascent is mapped: unattached understanding, self conquered, longing gone — by renunciation to the supreme perfection of actionlessness; then, in brief, the climb to Brahman: purified intellect, solitude, light food, governed speech and body, constant meditation, dispassion; egoism, force, arrogance, desire, anger, possession released — serene, become Brahman, one grieves not, craves not, equal to all beings — and attains supreme devotion to Me, by which alone I am known in truth, and entered.
verses.hook: How can you reach freedom from action while still working?

views.text: Saṁnyāsa is monasticism or the knowledge that precedes giving up all actions; naiṣkarmya is the state of one whose duties have fallen away on realising the actionless Brahman as his Self.
Saṁnyāsa equals tyāga: by seeing the Supreme Person as the true agent, one keeps acting and reaches the perfection beyond activity, namely steady meditation in which the senses cease.
Jitātmā means free of ego; acting without attachment or desire for fruit is already a kind of actionlessness, since there is no sense of being the doer, and it purifies sattva.
Actionlessness is reached amid worldly life by doing one's duty fully as worship while leaving outcomes to God, like a bridge untouched by the water flowing beneath it.

verses.devanagari:
सिद्धिं प्राप्तो यथा ब्रह्म तथाप्नोति निबोध मे ।
समासेनैव कौन्तेय निष्ठा ज्ञानस्य या परा॥
verses.transliteration:
siddhiṃ prāpto yathā brahma tathāpnoti nibodha me
samāsenaiva kaunteya niṣṭhā jñānasya yā parā
verses.essence: Learn from me in brief, Kaunteya, how one who has attained perfection reaches Brahman — that supreme consummation of knowledge.
verses.translation: Learn from Me in brief, O Arjuna, how he who has attained perfection reaches Brahman (the Eternal), that supreme state of knowledge.

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, nominative singular (one who has reached)
pronoun, genitive/ablative singular, short form (from me)
noun, masculine, instrumental singular (by way of)

verses.explanation: The final ascent announced: from siddhi — the ripeness won through consecrated work — to Brahman itself, the parā niṣṭhā, knowledge's last standing-place. What follows in 18.51–53 is the Gita's closing portrait of contemplative consummation: the ladder's top rungs, drawn samāsena, in spare, swift strokes.
verses.connection: Opens the three-verse ascent (18.51–53): from perfected action into the silence of Brahman.
verses.reflection: Set tonight's aim at the consummation: not better performance, but knowledge's final resting place.
verses.background: The final ascent is mapped: unattached understanding, self conquered, longing gone — by renunciation to the supreme perfection of actionlessness; then, in brief, the climb to Brahman: purified intellect, solitude, light food, governed speech and body, constant meditation, dispassion; egoism, force, arrogance, desire, anger, possession released — serene, become Brahman, one grieves not, craves not, equal to all beings — and attains supreme devotion to Me, by which alone I am known in truth, and entered.
verses.hook: How does one who is perfected in action go on to reach Brahman?

views.text: The siddhi already won is the fitness of body and organs for steadfastness in knowledge, given by God's grace; the 'consummation' is realising Brahman, which cannot be known as an object with form.
The perfection is success in meditation born from karma-yoga practised daily until death; the self is the final goal of knowledge, here understood as meditation.
Krishna gives the method only briefly; the actual technique of self-realisation has to be learnt directly from a guru.

Book knowledge is not realization; the karma yogi practises scriptural truths day and night, and on reaching actionlessness in work, transcendental knowledge comes through experience and leads to God-realization.

verses.devanagari:
बुद्ध्या विशुद्धया युक्तो धृत्यात्मानं नियम्य च ।
शब्दादीन्विषयांस्त्यक्त्वा रागद्वेषौ व्युदस्य च॥
verses.transliteration:
buddhyā viśuddhayā yukto dhṛtyātmānaṃ niyamya ca
śabdādīnviṣayāṃstyaktvā rāgadveṣau vyudasya ca
verses.essence: Endowed with a purified understanding, restraining the self with firmness, relinquishing sound and the other sense-objects, casting aside passion and hatred —
verses.translation: Endowed with a pure intellect, controlling the self by firmness, relinquishing sound and other objects and abandoning attraction and hatred.

anvaya.form: past passive participle, masculine, nominative singular

anvaya.parts: शब्द (sound) + आदि (and so on): 'beginning with sound'

anvaya.form: noun compound, masculine, accusative dual (object, the pair)
anvaya.parts: राग (attraction) + द्वेष (aversion): a pair compound

verses.explanation: The ascent's first stage gathers the chapter's own instruments: the buddhi of 18.30, now viśuddhā, scrubbed clear; the sattvic dhṛti of 18.33 as the holding force; the senses gently unplugged from their objects; and the two old magnets, rāga and dveṣa, set down at last. The climber travels light.
verses.connection: Stage one of the ascent: the inner equipment, purified and stilled.
verses.reflection: Travel light into one task today: judgment cleaned, grip steady, the two old magnets set down.
verses.background: The final ascent is mapped: unattached understanding, self conquered, longing gone — by renunciation to the supreme perfection of actionlessness; then, in brief, the climb to Brahman: purified intellect, solitude, light food, governed speech and body, constant meditation, dispassion; egoism, force, arrogance, desire, anger, possession released — serene, become Brahman, one grieves not, craves not, equal to all beings — and attains supreme devotion to Me, by which alone I am known in truth, and entered.
verses.hook: What inner discipline prepares a person to realize Brahman?

views.text: Giving up objects means giving up whatever exceeds bare bodily maintenance; casting off rāga and dveṣa applies even to the things that come to hand for keeping the body alive.
A purified understanding is one able to grasp the self as it really is; restraint by steadiness turns the mind away from outer and inner objects, making it fit for meditation.
The buddhi and dhṛti meant are the sattvic ones described earlier in the chapter; 'the self' restrained is that very buddhi made steady. The sentence runs on to 'fit for becoming Brahman' in 18.53.
The perfection needed for Brahman-realization begins with a purified intellect fixed in knowledge, a mind steadied by not indulging likes and dislikes, and senses firmly restrained.

verses.devanagari:
विविक्तसेवी लघ्वाशी यतवाक्कायमानसः ।
ध्यानयोगपरो नित्यं वैराग्यं समुपाश्रितः॥
verses.transliteration:
viviktasevī laghvāśī yatavākkāyamānasaḥ
dhyānayogaparo nityaṃ vairāgyaṃ samupāśritaḥ
verses.essence: — dwelling in solitude, eating lightly, with speech, body and mind governed, ever absorbed in the yoga of meditation, taking firm refuge in dispassion —
verses.translation: Dwelling in solitude, eating but little, with speech, body and mind subdued, always engaged in meditation and concentration, resorting to dispassion.

anvaya.base: विविक्त + सेविन् · secluded + one who frequents
anvaya.parts: विविक्त (solitary place) + सेवी (who resorts to): 'one who keeps to solitude'
लघु (light, little) + आशी (who eats): 'a light eater'

anvaya.meaning: with speech, body and mind controlled
anvaya.base: यत + वाच् + काय + मानस · restrained + speech + body + mind
anvaya.parts: यत (restrained) + वाक् (speech) + काय (body) + मानस (mind): 'one whose speech, body and mind are restrained'

anvaya.meaning: intent on the yoga of meditation
anvaya.base: ध्यान + योग + पर · meditation + yoga + devoted
anvaya.parts: ध्यान (meditation) + योग (yoga) + पर (having as highest): 'one for whom meditation-yoga is supreme'

anvaya.base: सम् + उप + आ + √श्रि · to resort to fully

verses.explanation: Stage two: the outer life pared to match the inner — solitude sought, the plate light, the three instruments of expression (voice, body, mind) under one governance, meditation no longer an appointment but the day's axis. Vairāgyaṁ samupāśritaḥ: dispassion not as deprivation but as *refuge* — the place one finally gets to rest.
verses.connection: Stage two: the simplified life of ch6's meditator, returning as the path's last mile.
verses.reflection: Simplify one outer thing today to match an inner intention — lighter plate, quieter hour, governed word.
verses.background: The final ascent is mapped: unattached understanding, self conquered, longing gone — by renunciation to the supreme perfection of actionlessness; then, in brief, the climb to Brahman: purified intellect, solitude, light food, governed speech and body, constant meditation, dispassion; egoism, force, arrogance, desire, anger, possession released — serene, become Brahman, one grieves not, craves not, equal to all beings — and attains supreme devotion to Me, by which alone I am known in truth, and entered.
verses.hook: What daily way of living supports deep meditation on the Absolute?

views.text: Solitude and light food are named because they calm the mind by removing sleep and similar defects; 'always' signals that meditation leaves no room for other duties such as mantra repetition.
Eat neither too much nor too little; meditate day after day until death; and build dispassion by seeing the defects in every object except the one meditated upon.
Dhyāna-yoga is contact with Brahman through meditation, and dispassion is relied on again and again so that the meditation is never broken.
Urges householders to spend a fortnight or a month a year in solitude at a holy place, with moderate food and periods of silence, instead of wasting holidays in the city.
Such a yogi keeps eating, sleeping, speech and body in balance, prefers solitude because of a contemplative nature, and keeps the mind constantly absorbed in the transcendent.

verses.devanagari:
अहंकारं बलं दर्पं कामं क्रोधं परिग्रहम् ।
विमुच्य निर्ममः शान्तो ब्रह्मभूयाय कल्पते॥
verses.transliteration:
ahaṃkāraṃ balaṃ darpaṃ kāmaṃ krodhaṃ parigraham
vimucya nirmamaḥ śānto brahmabhūyāya kalpate
verses.essence: — having abandoned egoism, force, arrogance, desire, anger and possession; free of 'mine', tranquil — one is fit for becoming Brahman.
verses.translation: Having abandoned egoism, strength, arrogance, desire, anger and covetousness, and free from the notion of 'mine' and peaceful, he is fit for becoming Brahman.

anvaya.parts: अहम् (I) + कार (making): 'the sense of I'
निर् (without) + मम (mine): 'one with no sense of mine'
ब्रह्म (Brahman) + भूय (becoming, from √भू): 'becoming Brahman'

verses.explanation: The last things set down — and they are the heavy ones: the I-knot itself, the will to force, the swagger, the old pair desire-and-anger, and parigraha, the instinct to accumulate and hold. What remains when all six are released is described in two words: nirmamaḥ śāntaḥ — nothing called mine, and peace. Such a one is kalpate, *fit*: Brahman-becoming is less an achievement than a fitness finally attained.
verses.connection: The ascent completes: emptied of the six weights, the climber and the summit are no longer two — 18.54 describes the view.
verses.reflection: Set down the heavy six where you find them today: I-knot, force, swagger, craving, anger, hoarding.
verses.background: The final ascent is mapped: unattached understanding, self conquered, longing gone — by renunciation to the supreme perfection of actionlessness; then, in brief, the climb to Brahman: purified intellect, solitude, light food, governed speech and body, constant meditation, dispassion; egoism, force, arrogance, desire, anger, possession released — serene, become Brahman, one grieves not, craves not, equal to all beings — and attains supreme devotion to Me, by which alone I am known in truth, and entered.
verses.hook: What must you let go of to become fit to realize Brahman?

views.text: Bala is the force tied to desire, not natural bodily strength; dropping parigraha means giving up even gifts for bodily upkeep, becoming a paramahaṁsa monk with no 'mine' even toward his own body.
Śānta means finding one's sole happiness in experiencing the self; freed from all bonds, such a meditator experiences the self as it really is.
Ahaṁkāra includes the pride 'I am detached'; brahma-bhūya is remaining unshaken in the certainty 'I am Brahman'.
In this stage the ego with its craving for power and prestige dissolves, and the yogi becomes tranquil and free of desire, anger and greed, ready to realize Brahman.

verses.devanagari:
ब्रह्मभूतः प्रसन्नात्मा न शोचति न काङ्क्षति ।
समः सर्वेषु भूतेषु मद्भक्तिं लभते पराम्॥
verses.transliteration:
brahmabhūtaḥ prasannātmā na śocati na kāṅkṣati
samaḥ sarveṣu bhūteṣu madbhaktiṃ labhate parām
verses.essence: Having become Brahman, serene in self, one neither grieves nor desires; equal toward all beings, one attains supreme devotion to me.
verses.translation: Becoming Brahman, serene in the Self, he neither grieves nor desires, the same to all beings, he obtains supreme devotion to Me.

anvaya.parts: ब्रह्म (Brahman) + भूत (become, from √भू) — "one who has become Brahman"

anvaya.base: प्रसन्नात्मन् · one whose self is clear
anvaya.parts: प्रसन्न (clear, serene) + आत्मन् (self) — "one whose self is serene"

anvaya.form: pronominal adjective, neuter, locative plural (toward, among)

anvaya.parts: मत् (me) + भक्ति (devotion) — "devotion directed to me"

anvaya.form: adjective, feminine, accusative singular (agrees with devotion)

verses.explanation: The Gita's great surprise, placed at the summit: brahma-bhūtaḥ — having *become* Brahman, serene, beyond grief and craving, equal to all beings — and what does such a one attain? Mad-bhaktiṁ parām: supreme devotion to me. Devotion is not the ladder discarded at the top; it is what the top opens into. Readings differ on what this highest devotion is: for Shankara it is knowledge itself in its fullness, the 'fourth' kind of devotee of 7.16; for Ramanuja it is love of the Lord made vivid beyond all description. All agree on the shock of the sequence: union does not end the relationship but perfects it.
verses.connection: The summit's disclosure: jnana flowers into bhakti — inverting every assumption that knowledge outgrows love.
verses.reflection: Watch grief and craving both go quiet for one moment — and notice love rising in the cleared space.
verses.background: The final ascent is mapped: unattached understanding, self conquered, longing gone — by renunciation to the supreme perfection of actionlessness; then, in brief, the climb to Brahman: purified intellect, solitude, light food, governed speech and body, constant meditation, dispassion; egoism, force, arrogance, desire, anger, possession released — serene, become Brahman, one grieves not, craves not, equal to all beings — and attains supreme devotion to Me, by which alone I am known in truth, and entered.
verses.hook: What happens after a person fully realizes Brahman?

refs.note: Even sages who rejoice in the self and are free of all bonds still feel drawn to devotion, because God's qualities attract the liberated, showing bhakti follows realization.
The four Kumaras, absorbed in formless Brahman, pray they would accept even hell if their minds could relish the Lord's lotus feet, showing knowers turn to devotion.

views.text: Treats the supreme devotion as knowledge itself, the devotion of the 'fourth' kind of devotee, the wise one of 7.16. 'Equal to all' means judging others' joy and pain by one's own standard.

Becoming Brahman means knowing the self as pure knowledge and as belonging to the Lord; such a one finds everything but the Lord as worthless as straw, and reaches a love that makes the Lord dear beyond words.
Reads 'equal to all' as tender compassion: feeling others' pain and joy as one's own, with jealousy and the sense of separateness gone.

Brahman-realization brings serenity and equal vision, yet the verse ends with a twist: the realized soul then attains supreme devotion, so bhakti is not merely a step toward knowledge but its fulfilment.

verses.devanagari:
भक्त्या मामभिजानाति यावान्यश्चास्मि तत्त्वतः ।
ततो मां तत्त्वतो ज्ञात्वा विशते तदनन्तरम्॥
verses.transliteration:
bhaktyā māmabhijānāti yāvānyaścāsmi tattvataḥ
tato māṃ tattvato jñātvā viśate tadanantaram
verses.essence: By devotion one knows me in truth — how great I am and who I am. Then, knowing me in truth, one enters into me forthwith.
verses.translation: By devotion he knows Me in truth, what and who I am; then having known Me in truth, he forthwith enters into the Supreme.

anvaya.form: noun, feminine, instrumental singular (by means of)

anvaya.base: यावत् · as much as, how great

anvaya.parts: तत् (that) + अनन्तरम् (with no interval) — "immediately after that"

verses.explanation: The epistemology of love, completing 18.54: bhaktyā mām abhijānāti — by devotion one knows him *tattvataḥ*, as he actually is, in both extent (yāvān) and identity (yaḥ). Analysis circles the fortress; love is handed the key. And then the verb 11.54 promised: viśate — one *enters*. Knower into Known, lover into Beloved: the Gita's final account of liberation is an entering.
verses.connection: Twins with 11.54: love as the one instrument that knows God whole — and the door through which one passes in.
verses.reflection: Let love be your method of knowing once today — study someone or something by cherishing it.
verses.background: The final ascent is mapped: unattached understanding, self conquered, longing gone — by renunciation to the supreme perfection of actionlessness; then, in brief, the climb to Brahman: purified intellect, solitude, light food, governed speech and body, constant meditation, dispassion; egoism, force, arrogance, desire, anger, possession released — serene, become Brahman, one grieves not, craves not, equal to all beings — and attains supreme devotion to Me, by which alone I am known in truth, and entered.
verses.hook: How can anyone come to know who God truly is?

refs.note: Brahma Vidyā herself, full of Brahman's bliss, does austerities to gain love for Krishna and feels empty without it, showing knowledge alone cannot reveal God's personal form.

views.text: 'How great I am' is the Lord as he appears through many limiting adjuncts; 'who I am' is him with all of them gone: one, pure consciousness. Knowing and entering are not two acts; the knowing is itself the entering.
Devotion shows the Lord's essence and his attributes; that vision then ripens into an even greater, unsurpassed devotion, and it is through that devotion that one enters him, as 11.54 said.
Entering comes when even this knowledge falls quiet: one simply becomes the supreme bliss.
The personal form of God, with his virtues and pastimes, cannot be known through action, knowledge or yoga; love alone opens that door, for devotees see God with the eyes of love.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वकर्माण्यपि सदा कुर्वाणो मद्व्यपाश्रयः ।
मत्प्रसादादवाप्नोति शाश्वतं पदमव्ययम्॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvakarmāṇyapi sadā kurvāṇo madvyapāśrayaḥ
matprasādādavāpnoti śāśvataṃ padamavyayam
verses.essence: Even while performing all actions, one who takes refuge in me attains, by my grace, the eternal imperishable abode.

verses.explanation: The teaching descends from the summit back to the street, deliberately: sarva-karmāṇy api sadā kurvāṇaḥ — doing *everything, always* — the full working life, untrimmed. The two operative words: mad-vyapāśrayaḥ, refuge taken in him, and mat-prasādāt, *by my grace*. Effort builds the readiness; grace closes the distance. The eternal abode, reached without ever leaving one's post.
verses.connection: Reassures the householder after the renunciate's ascent: the same destination, reached amid all duties, by refuge and grace.
verses.reflection: Keep every duty and take refuge anyway — the eternal abode is reached without leaving your post.
verses.background: The teaching narrows to its personal close: doing all actions always, taking refuge in Me, by My grace one gains the eternal abode — so mentally resign all acts to Me and be ever-minded of Me: you shall cross every difficulty by My grace; but if from egoism you will not listen, you shall perish. Your own nature will compel what delusion now refuses; the Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, whirling them as if mounted on a machine. To Him surrender with your whole being. Thus the knowledge more secret than all secrets has been declared: reflect on it fully — then act as you choose.
verses.hook: Can you reach God's eternal abode while still carrying out your work?

views.text: 'All actions' is pressed to include even forbidden ones: whoever has wholly surrendered to the Lord still reaches the state of Vishnu, by grace.
Refuge means handing one's agency to the Lord; then even rites done for wished-for ends, offered as worship without the wish, lead to the same goal as the obligatory duties.
Devotees do not give up work but give up the pride of being doers, seeing all work as service to God; after death they reach the divine abode of the form they worship.

verses.explanation: The whole path, issued as one personal instruction: cetasā — *with the mind* — deposit every action in him as it happens; keep him as the pole-star (mat-paraḥ); steady it all with buddhi-yoga, the disciplined understanding of chapter 2; and the summary imperative: mac-cittaḥ satataṁ bhava — be, continuously, one whose thought rests in me. Four moves, one life.
verses.connection: The teaching turns imperative and intimate — the prescription whose promise and warning follow in 18.58.
verses.reflection: Run the four moves through one hour: deposit acts in Him, face Him, steady the buddhi, remember.

verses.hook: How should you hold your mind and actions toward God?

views.text: Surrender is to be done 'with the mind', with discernment, in the spirit of 9.27; buddhi-yoga is keeping the intellect fixed on the Lord alone, with no other support.
'With the mind' means knowing the self as the Lord's own and ruled by him; buddhi-yoga is the seeker's settled attitude toward agency and fruits while all acts go on.
Buddhi yoga means an intellect firmly convinced that everything comes from God and exists for his pleasure; since the intellect governs the mind, training it this way lets the heart attach to God.

verses.translation: Fixing thy mind on Me, thou shalt by My grace overcome all obstacles; but if from egoism thou wilt not hear Me, thou shalt perish.

verses.explanation: Promise and warning in perfect symmetry: mac-cittaḥ... tariṣyasi — mind in him, every durga, every fortress-like strait, crossed on grace; ahaṅkārāt... vinaṅkṣyasi — ego at the helm, ruin. The blunt second clause is love refusing to flatter: the stakes on this battlefield, and in every life, are real. The next verses show exactly *how* the ego's refusal would play out.
verses.connection: The fork stated plainly — and 18.59–60 walks down the refusal-branch to show where it leads.
verses.reflection: Stand at the fork consciously once today: mind-on-Him crosses everything; ego at the helm sinks.

verses.hook: What happens if you rely on God, and what if pride refuses?

views.text: The egoism is the thought 'I am learned', and with it 'I am independent, why follow another's bidding?' The difficulties are all the causes of rebirth.
The conceit is 'I know what should and should not be done'; but only the Lord knows this for all beings and gives them their law.
The soul is never independent of God: taking full shelter with the mind on him dissolves every obstacle by grace, but ignoring his guidance out of vanity means missing life's goal.

verses.devanagari:
यदहंकारमाश्रित्य न योत्स्य इति मन्यसे ।
मिथ्यैष व्यवसायस्ते प्रकृतिस्त्वां नियोक्ष्यति॥
verses.transliteration:
yadahaṃkāramāśritya na yotsya iti manyase
mithyaiṣa vyavasāyaste prakṛtistvāṃ niyokṣyati
verses.essence: If, taking refuge in egoism, you think 'I will not fight' — vain is this resolve of yours: your own nature will compel you.
verses.translation: If, filled with egoism, thou thinkest: "I will not fight", vain is this, thy resolve; Nature will compel thee.

anvaya.form: relative pronoun, neuter, used as a conjunction (that, if)

anvaya.base: thus (marks a quotation or a reason)

verses.explanation: The refusal-branch examined: na yotsye, 'I will not fight' — the very sentence of 2.9 — diagnosed as a decision made *by the ego about a nature it does not command*. Mithyā, void: a kshatriya's marrow, a lifetime in the making, will not be vetoed by an afternoon's anguish. Prakṛtis tvāṁ niyokṣyati — what you are will overrule what you currently prefer.
verses.connection: Dismantles 2.9's refusal with chapter 18's psychology: temperament outvotes mood.
verses.reflection: Catch one 'I will not' that your own nature is already overruling — and choose your relation to it.

verses.hook: Can you simply refuse to act against your own nature?

views.text: The nature that will impel him is plainly his own nature as a kshatriya.
The ego here is a false sense of independence; whoever ignores the Lord's command and resolves by himself will be driven against that resolve by nature.
The resolve is vain because Arjuna is not independent: nature, in the form of rajas, will push him into battle.
We lack absolute freedom: our nature, shaped by the modes, compels us to act, so the real choice is between God's guidance and our compulsions, like a retired soldier snapping to attention.

verses.devanagari:
स्वभावजेन कौन्तेय निबद्धः स्वेन कर्मणा ।
कर्तुं नेच्छसि यन्मोहात्करिष्यस्यवशोपि तत्॥

svabhāvajena kaunteya nibaddhaḥ svena karmaṇā
kartuṃ necchasi yanmohātkariṣyasyavaśopi tat
verses.essence: Bound by your own duty born of your nature, Kaunteya — what from delusion you wish not to do, that you shall do even against your will.
verses.translation: O Arjuna, bound by thy own Karma (action) born of thy own nature, that which from delusion thou wishest not to do, even that thou shalt do helplessly.

anvaya.parts: स्वभाव (one's own nature) + ज (born) — "born of one's nature"

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, ablative singular (from, out of)

verses.explanation: The argument completed without a single appeal to heaven: svabhāva-jena... nibaddhaḥ — bound by your own born nature, the war will pull you in avaśaḥ, will-or-no, once the first arrow flies past your brother. The only live choice is *how* you will be in it: dragged by compulsion, or upright in consecration. Freedom, the Gita has taught throughout, is not choosing your nature but choosing your relation to it.
verses.connection: Closes the compulsion-argument — and 18.61 reveals the deeper hand turning all natures.
verses.reflection: What you are will out — so consecrate it today rather than be dragged by it.

verses.hook: Will Arjuna's warrior nature push him to fight anyway?

views.text: Svabhāva means the tendencies laid down by good and bad acts of past births, which shape one's present duties; here it is heroism and the like named in 18.43.
Pictures the mechanism concretely: stung by the enemy's taunts, Arjuna's warrior nature will overpower his present reluctance.
Acting only on the push of one's nature binds through merit and demerit; acting by the knowledge Krishna has taught, the same acts no longer bind.
Arjun's warrior tendencies from past lives will not let him stand idle before injustice, so it is better for him to fight by Krishna's instruction than be driven to it by his nature.

verses.explanation: The vista widens to its furthest edge: īśvaraḥ... hṛd-deśe tiṣṭhati — the Lord stationed in the heart-region of every being, turning all beings by his māyā as figures yantrārūḍhāni, mounted on a machine. Nature itself, which 18.60 said compels you, is itself being turned. The commentators press the image differently: for Ramanuja the machine is the body and senses, set moving by the Lord according to each being's guṇas; for Śrīdhara it is a puppeteer working wooden figures. The image humbles utterly — and prepares the most tender pivot in the poem: the Turner is not above the machine but inside the rider, so he can be *gone to*. The next verse says: go to him.
verses.connection: The final metaphysical frame: behind svabhava stands its Lord — making 18.62's surrender the obvious door.
verses.reflection: Remember mid-commotion: the Turner of all this machinery is seated in your own heart — visit Him there.

verses.hook: Where does the Lord dwell, and how does he move all beings?

views.text: Arjuna is addressed as 'white', pure of mind; the Lord resides in the heart while turning beings like wooden figures on a machine, the word 'as if' being understood.
The heart is the seat of all knowledge behind every act; the machine is the body and senses the Lord himself made, and he moves beings according to their guṇas.
Śrīdhara calls the earlier two verses the view of other schools, and this the Lord's own: the inner ruler turns beings like a puppeteer working wooden figures.
The body is a machine made of God's energy and given according to past karma; God sits within it noting every thought and deed, so the soul is never independent and should surrender.

verses.explanation: The instruction the whole chapter has been narrowing toward: tam eva śaraṇaṁ gaccha — go to *him* alone for refuge, sarva-bhāvena, with everything you are, holding nothing in reserve. The third person points to the Lord in the heart of 18.61 — yet the commentators hear no distance in it: the Lord in the heart is the one speaking from the chariot, and the eternal abode is his own supreme state. Grace answers wholeness: tat-prasādāt, by his grace, parā śānti, the supreme peace, and the abode that does not pass.
verses.connection: The penultimate instruction — whose first-person form, the Gita's last word, waits at 18.66.
verses.reflection: Surrender with the whole being once today — sarva-bhavena — nothing held back in reserve.

verses.hook: What does complete surrender to the Lord bring you?

refs.note: A seeker of liberation takes shelter of the Supreme who created Brahma and gave the Vedas, by whose grace the self and intellect are illumined.
Krishna tells Uddhava to give up all conventions and take refuge in him alone, the Soul of all, to cross the material ocean and become fearless.
The moment the soul turns toward God in surrender, the sins of countless past lives are destroyed by his grace.

views.text: Take refuge in the Lord alone, with one's whole being, to be rid of worldly suffering; by God's grace one attains the highest tranquillity and the eternal Abode, the supreme State of Viṣṇu.
Refuge means giving body, senses and mind to the charioteer who commands 'act thus'; the fighting is unavoidable either way, so fight in the way he has taught.
When the real doer and knower, one's own Self, is held in the heart, the effects of action find no footing, as deer-calves stay still while a lion-cub dwells in the nearby cave.
Since all beings depend on the Lord, give up egoism and go to him with your whole self; his grace brings peace and his eternal abode.
Self-effort alone cannot free the soul; only God's grace can, and that grace follows a rational rule rather than whim: it is given to those who qualify by surrendering to him.

verses.devanagari:
इति ते ज्ञानमाख्यातं गुह्याद्गुह्यतरं मया ।

vimṛśyaitadaśeṣeṇa yathecchasi tathā kuru
verses.essence: Thus has this knowledge, more secret than all secrets, been declared to you by me. Reflect on it fully — then act as you choose.
verses.translation: Thus has wisdom, more secret than secrecy itself, been declared unto thee by Me; having reflected over it fully, then act as thou wishest.

verses.explanation: The teaching ends by handing back the wheel: iti te jñānam ākhyātam — thus has this knowledge, guhyād guhyataram, more secret than any secret, been declared — then vimṛśyaitad aśeṣeṇa: think it through, *all* of it, and yathecchasi tathā kuru, do as you choose. God himself declines to compel the heart he made free; the teaching asks to be thought through, not merely obeyed. The commentators read the freedom in their own ways: Ramanuja as leave to take up karma, jñāna or bhakti yoga as one is fitted; Śrīdhara as confidence that once it is pondered, delusion will fall away on its own. The granted liberty prepares 18.73's freely spoken 'I will act.'
verses.connection: The release of the reins — the precondition for 18.73's freely-spoken 'I will act.'
verses.reflection: Honor your own freedom as God honors it: deliberate fully today, then choose — yathecchasi tatha kuru.

verses.hook: After hearing all this teaching, who makes the final choice?

refs.note: Rama, after teaching the people of Ayodhya, says his advice is neither wrong nor coercive: listen, reflect and then do as you wish, echoing Krishna's freedom given to Arjun.

views.text: The omniscient God has imparted knowledge more secret than any secret, extremely profound; Arjuna should ponder the whole Scripture and all its subjects, and then act as he likes.
'Do as you wish' means: having weighed it all, take up karma, jñāna or bhakti yoga according to your fitness and liking.
It is more secret than the Upanishads because it reveals the supreme non-duality; the teacher repeats because the mind is never sated when the choicest thing is explained.
Krishna speaks as the all-knowing and supremely compassionate; once the whole Gita is pondered, Arjuna's delusion will fall away of itself.
Having taught the most secret knowledge, Krishna leaves the choice to Arjun, because God gives souls limited free will; love requires choice, so even God will not force the soul to surrender.

verses.devanagari:

iṣṭo'si me dṛḍhamiti tato vakṣyāmi te hitam
verses.essence: Hear again my supreme word, most secret of all. You are surely beloved of me — therefore I will speak for your good.
verses.translation: Hear thou again My supreme word, most secret of all; because thou art dearly beloved of Me, I will tell thee what is good.

verses.explanation: Having set Arjuna free, Krishna cannot quite stop — and the reason given is the whole theology of the Gita in one clause: iṣṭo 'si me dṛḍham, *you are firmly dear to me*. The final secret is not earned by qualification; it overflows from affection. What follows (18.65–66) is spoken not from the teacher's chair but from the friend's heart.
verses.connection: Love overriding the closure of 18.63 — the preface to the Gita's two culminating verses.
verses.reflection: Hear the reason behind every teaching you have received: you are firmly dear. Let that be the lens.
verses.background: What freedom released, love calls back: hear once more My supreme word, most secret of all — you are firmly beloved of Me, therefore I speak your good. Fix your mind on Me, be devoted, sacrifice, bow — you shall come to Me; truly I promise, you are dear to Me. Then the carama-shloka, the Gita's last teaching-word: abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in Me alone; I will release you from all sins — do not grieve.
verses.hook: Why does Krishna share his deepest teaching with Arjuna?

views.text: Not from fear or for gain does the Lord speak, but because Arjuna is dear; the good he will tell is the highest means to knowledge.
The most secret of all is bhakti yoga, already so called at 9.1; it is repeated now because Arjuna is exceedingly dear.
Seeing that Arjuna cannot ponder the whole deep teaching, Krishna himself gathers its essence out of compassion. Śrīdhara also notes a reading 'dṛḍhamatiḥ', firm of mind.
A teacher reveals the deepest secret only when the student is ready; having seen Arjun grasp the teaching so well, Krishna shares the final truth because Arjun is dear to him.

verses.devanagari:

मामेवैष्यसि सत्यं ते प्रतिजाने प्रियोऽसि मे॥
