māmevaiṣyasi satyaṃ te pratijāne priyo'si me
verses.essence: Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, sacrifice to me, bow to me — and you shall come to me alone. Truly I promise you: you are dear to me.
verses.translation: Fix thy mind on Me, by devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, bow down to Me. Thou shalt come even to Me; truly do I promise unto thee, (for) thou art dear to Me.

anvaya.base: मन्मनस् · one whose mind is on me
anvaya.parts: मत् (me) + मनस् (mind) — "one whose mind is on me"
मत् (me) + भक्त (devoted) — "one devoted to me"

anvaya.base: मद्याजिन् · one who sacrifices to me
anvaya.parts: मत् (me) + याजिन् (one who offers sacrifice) — "one who worships me"

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, accusative singular used as adverb (truly)

verses.explanation: The first line of 9.34 returns word for word — mind, love, worship, reverence, all aimed at one address — but now sealed with what 9.34 did not have: satyaṁ te pratijāne, *I promise you, truly*. The Absolute giving its word, and giving the reason: priyo 'si me, you are dear to me. Ramanuja draws out the logic: one who loves the Lord beyond measure is held dear beyond measure, and the Lord, unable to bear separation, himself brings that one home. The whole apparatus of yoga compressed into a relationship between two who hold each other dear.
verses.connection: 9.34 repeated and notarized — the promise that 18.66 will raise to its absolute form.
verses.reflection: Do the four before sleep — mind on Him, love to Him, an offering, a bow — and rest on a promise.
verses.background: What freedom released, love calls back: hear once more My supreme word, most secret of all — you are firmly beloved of Me, therefore I speak your good. Fix your mind on Me, be devoted, sacrifice, bow — you shall come to Me; truly I promise, you are dear to Me. Then the carama-shloka, the Gita's last teaching-word: abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in Me alone; I will release you from all sins — do not grieve.
verses.hook: What does Krishna ask of the one who wants to reach him?

refs.note: King Ambarisha engaged mind, speech, hands, eyes and every sense in serving Krishna without selfish motive, a model of the total absorption in devotion this verse asks for.

views.text: Knowing the Lord is true to his promise, and that liberation surely follows devotion, one should make dedication to God the single supreme goal.
'Mind on me' is the meditation the Upanishads enjoin: a steady stream of loving remembrance. The Lord, unable to bear separation from such a lover, himself brings him home.
The line shows that the whole weight of scripture lies in offering everything to Brahman; the Gita serves one who cultivates that dedication.
Krishna repeats his call to exclusive, loving devotion, the essence of all scripture, but this is not yet the supreme secret, which he reveals in the next verse.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वधर्मान्परित्यज्य मामेकं शरणं व्रज ।
अहं त्वा सर्वपापेभ्यो मोक्षयिष्यामि मा शुचः॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvadharmānparityajya māmekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja
ahaṃ tvā sarvapāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ
verses.essence: Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone. I will release you from all sins — do not grieve.
verses.translation: Abandoning all duties, take refuge in Me alone: I will liberate thee from all sins; grieve not.

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + धर्म (duty, righteous practice) — "all dharmas"

anvaya.form: adjective, masculine, accusative singular (agrees with me)

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + पाप (sin) — "all sins"

anvaya.form: verb, aorist, 2nd person singular, used with मा (a prohibition)

verses.explanation: The carama-śloka, the 'final verse' — the summit the tradition says the whole Gita climbs toward. Sarva-dharmān parityajya: release even the dharmas, the sacred scaffolding itself — not into lawlessness but into the One the laws were always pointing at. The commentators part ways on what is released: for Shankara, all action, right and wrong alike, in the knowledge of the one Self; for Ramanuja, the sense of being the doer and the claim on fruits — or, in his second reading, the expiations one feels unfit to finish. Then the promise: ahaṁ tvā sarva-pāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi — *I* will free you, from *all* of it. And mā śucaḥ, grieve no more — the grief that felled the archer in chapter 1, finally addressed.
verses.connection: The Gita's last teaching-word: every path released into pure refuge — the answer to 1.47's weeping archer.
verses.reflection: When every framework fails today, use the final verse as it was given: one refuge, all burdens lifted, grieve not.
verses.background: What freedom released, love calls back: hear once more My supreme word, most secret of all — you are firmly beloved of Me, therefore I speak your good. Fix your mind on Me, be devoted, sacrifice, bow — you shall come to Me; truly I promise, you are dear to Me. Then the carama-shloka, the Gita's last teaching-word: abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in Me alone; I will release you from all sins — do not grieve.
verses.hook: What is Krishna's final instruction, and what does he promise in return?

refs.note: One who fully surrenders to Mukunda owes nothing to gods, sages, ancestors, humans or other beings, so leaving worldly duties for God incurs no sin.
Those who see the limits of prescribed duties, give them all up and worship God alone are counted the best of seekers.

views.text: 'All dharmas' includes adharma: what is meant is renouncing all action, knowing there is nothing besides the one Self. The Lord frees by revealing his nature, and knowledge alone is the means to liberation.
Two readings: give up the sense of agency, possession and fruit in all practice, seeing the Lord as doer and goal; or give up the endless expiations that seem to bar one from starting bhakti.
Do not own the slaying of kinsmen as 'I am the doer', nor count avoiding it as merit; take the Lord, the agent of all acts, as guardian of your natural impulses.
With firm faith that devotion alone will accomplish everything, give up servitude to injunctions; fear no sin for leaving rites aside, since the Lord himself will free you.
Krishna now reverses his earlier counsel: one may renounce all bodily duties and surrender to God alone, since devotion is the soul's true dharma and serving God fulfils every other debt.

verses.devanagari:
इदं ते नातपस्काय नाभक्ताय कदाचन ।
न चाशुश्रूषवे वाच्यं न च मां योऽभ्यसूयति॥
verses.transliteration:
idaṃ te nātapaskāya nābhaktāya kadācana
na cāśuśrūṣave vācyaṃ na ca māṃ yo'bhyasūyati
verses.essence: This is never to be spoken by you to one without austerity, nor to one without devotion, nor to one unwilling to hear, nor to one who speaks ill of me.
verses.translation: This is never to be spoken by thee to one who is devoid of austerities or devotion, nor to one who does not render service or who does not desire to listen, nor to one who cavils at Me.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + तपस् (austerity) + क — "one without austerity"
अ (not) + भक्त (devoted) — "one who is not devoted"

anvaya.meaning: to one unwilling to listen or serve
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + शुश्रूषु (wishing to hear, eager to serve; desiderative of √श्रु) — "one with no wish to listen"

anvaya.form: gerundive, neuter, nominative singular (should be spoken)

verses.explanation: After the widest door, a guardian's word: the teaching is not to be pressed on the unready — the undisciplined, the loveless, the unwilling ear, the sneerer. Not elitism but ecology: seed scattered on scorn grows resentment, not freedom. The deepest things keep their own counsel until asked for; reverence is the soil this scripture germinates in.
verses.connection: The transmission-ethic: 18.66's open secret protected from contempt, kept for the thirsty.
verses.reflection: Guard the deepest things today — share them where there is thirst, not where there is sport.
verses.background: The transmission ethic is given: this is not to be spoken to one without austerity or devotion, to the unwilling ear, or the scoffer — but whoever declares this supreme secret among My devotees, showing highest love to Me, shall come to Me without doubt; none does Me dearer service, none on earth shall be dearer. Who studies this dialogue worships Me by the sacrifice of knowledge; even the faithful hearer, free of scoffing, is liberated to the bright worlds.
verses.hook: To whom should this deepest teaching not be given?

refs.note: Giving transcendental instruction to the faithless and those averse to God makes them offenders, which is why listeners' fitness must be checked.

views.text: Lays down the rule of transmission: teach one who is devoted, serves the teacher and does not cavil, whether austere or intelligent; never one who sneers at the Lord as an ordinary man.
The change of construction in the last clause marks the one who finds fault with the Lord as the worst of the four.
Reads the list as a sequence: austerity cuts sin, faith is born, the wish to listen keeps it from flashing and dying like lightning; contempt for the Lord disqualifies all.
Renouncing duties is only for those established in love of God, and a guru must judge who is eligible; given to the faithless or envious, the teaching harms rather than helps.

verses.devanagari:
य इदं परमं गुह्यं मद्भक्तेष्वभिधास्यति ।
भक्तिं मयि परां कृत्वा मामेवैष्यत्यसंशयः॥
verses.transliteration:
ya idaṃ paramaṃ guhyaṃ madbhakteṣvabhidhāsyati
bhaktiṃ mayi parāṃ kṛtvā māmevaiṣyatyasaṃśayaḥ
verses.essence: One who declares this supreme secret among my devotees, having shown highest devotion to me, shall come to me alone — there is no doubt.
verses.translation: He who with supreme devotion to Me will teach this supreme secret to My devotees, shall doubtlessly come to Me.

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, neuter, accusative singular (object)

anvaya.parts: मत् (me) + भक्त (devoted) — "those devoted to me"

anvaya.form: adjective, feminine, accusative singular (agrees with devotion)

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + संशय (doubt) — "free of doubt, doubtless"

verses.explanation: The flip side of the guard: among the thirsty, *pour*. To unfold this conversation for devoted hearts is itself ranked as parā bhakti, the highest act of love toward him — the teacher of the Gita performs devotion in the teaching. And the wage is the destination itself: mām evaiṣyati, sealed with asaṁśayaḥ — no doubt.
verses.connection: Sharing the teaching as worship — the verse behind every Gita discourse given since.
verses.reflection: Pass one verse of this book to a heart that needs it — the sharing is itself ranked as supreme love.
verses.background: The transmission ethic is given: this is not to be spoken to one without austerity or devotion, to the unwilling ear, or the scoffer — but whoever declares this supreme secret among My devotees, showing highest love to Me, shall come to Me without doubt; none does Me dearer service, none on earth shall be dearer. Who studies this dialogue worships Me by the sacrifice of knowledge; even the faithful hearer, free of scoffing, is liberated to the bright worlds.
verses.hook: What happens to one who shares this teaching with devotees?

views.text: The teacher hands on text and meaning in the attitude 'I am serving the Lord, the supreme Teacher'; that the hearers are called devotees shows devotion alone qualifies one to be taught.
Explaining the Gita among devotees is itself the cultivation of devotion, and the promise of union is a real injunction about the result, not mere praise.
Helping others take up devotion is an even greater blessing than doing it oneself and draws God's special grace; those who share the Gita's knowledge attain supreme devotion and then reach him.

verses.devanagari:
न च तस्मान्मनुष्येषु कश्चिन्मे प्रियकृत्तमः ।
भविता न च मे तस्मादन्यः प्रियतरो भुवि॥
verses.transliteration:
na ca tasmānmanuṣyeṣu kaścinme priyakṛttamaḥ
bhavitā na ca me tasmādanyaḥ priyataro bhuvi
verses.essence: Nor is there among humans any who does what is more dear to me than such a one; nor shall there be another on earth dearer to me.
verses.translation: Nor is there any among men who does dearer service to Me, nor shall there be another on earth dearer to Me than he.

anvaya.base: प्रियकृत्तम · best doer of what is dear
anvaya.parts: प्रिय (dear) + कृत् (doer) + तम (most) — "one who most does what is dear"

verses.explanation: A superlative and a comparative together, a very strong commendation: priya-kṛt-tamaḥ — of all human beings, none does him a *dearer service* than the one who carries this dialogue to hearts that need it; and none, now or to come, will be priya-taraḥ, dearer. The Gita ranks its own transmission as the supreme act of love — because what is handed over is the way home itself.
verses.connection: The strongest commendation in the text — reserved for the sharer of 18.68.
verses.reflection: Know the value of the carrier: no dearer service exists than handing someone the way home.
verses.background: The transmission ethic is given: this is not to be spoken to one without austerity or devotion, to the unwilling ear, or the scoffer — but whoever declares this supreme secret among My devotees, showing highest love to Me, shall come to Me without doubt; none does Me dearer service, none on earth shall be dearer. Who studies this dialogue worships Me by the sacrifice of knowledge; even the faithful hearer, free of scoffing, is liberated to the bright worlds.
verses.hook: Whom does Krishna hold dearer than anyone else on earth?

views.text: Answers an objection: even a seeker of liberation, devoted to meditation, has a duty to pass this teaching on to a qualified pupil.
None among men, now or later, gives the Lord greater delight than one who explains the Gita to his devotees.
Spiritual knowledge is among the highest gifts because it transforms people forever, so sharing the Gita is the dearest service to God, though teachers should see themselves only as his instruments.

verses.devanagari:
अध्येष्यते च य इमं धर्म्यं संवादमावयोः ।
ज्ञानयज्ञेन तेनाहमिष्टः स्यामिति मे मतिः॥
verses.transliteration:
adhyeṣyate ca ya imaṃ dharmyaṃ saṃvādamāvayoḥ
jñānayajñena tenāhamiṣṭaḥ syāmiti me matiḥ
verses.essence: And one who studies this dharma-filled dialogue of ours — by that one I shall be worshiped through the sacrifice of knowledge. So I hold.
verses.translation: And he who will study this sacred dialogue of ours, by him I shall have been worshipped by the sacrifice of wisdom, such is My conviction.

anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + यज्ञ (sacrifice) — "a sacrifice made of knowledge"

anvaya.base: thus (marks a quotation or a reason)

verses.explanation: The promise widens to every future reader: saṁvādam āvayoḥ — *our* dialogue, the conversation itself sanctified as text — and its study declared a jñāna-yajña, the sacrifice of knowledge that 4.33 ranked above all offerings of substance. Whoever opens these chapters, in any century, in any tongue, is performing worship; the reading you are doing now is, by this verse, a rite.
verses.connection: Consecrates the act of reading the Gita itself — fulfilling 4.33's hierarchy of sacrifice.
verses.reflection: Read even one verse today as rite, not consumption — by this chapter, your reading is worship.
verses.background: The transmission ethic is given: this is not to be spoken to one without austerity or devotion, to the unwilling ear, or the scoffer — but whoever declares this supreme secret among My devotees, showing highest love to Me, shall come to Me without doubt; none does Me dearer service, none on earth shall be dearer. Who studies this dialogue worships Me by the sacrifice of knowledge; even the faithful hearer, free of scoffing, is liberated to the bright worlds.
verses.hook: How is studying this dialogue a way of worshipping God?

views.text: Among ritual, loud, whispered and mental worship, the knowledge-sacrifice is best because it is mental; so study of the Gita is praised as that sacrifice. Or the verse may simply state the study's result.
Even one who recites without grasping the meaning is heard by the Lord as calling him, as with Ajāmila, who was saved by merely uttering the name.
Surrendering the intellect to God does not mean ceasing to think but using it fully to carry out his will, which the Gita reveals; studying it is thus worship with the intellect.

verses.devanagari:
श्रद्धावाननसूयश्च शृणुयादपि यो नरः ।
सोऽपि मुक्तः शुभाँल्लोकान्प्राप्नुयात्पुण्यकर्मणाम्॥
verses.transliteration:
śraddhāvānanasūyaśca śṛṇuyādapi yo naraḥ
so'pi muktaḥ śubhāṃllokānprāpnuyātpuṇyakarmaṇām
verses.essence: And even the one who, full of faith and without scoffing, simply hears it — that one too, liberated, shall attain the radiant worlds of the righteous.
verses.translation: Also the man who hears this, full of faith and free from malice, he, too, liberated, shall attain to the happy worlds of those of righteous deeds.

anvaya.parts: अन् (not) + असूया (fault-finding, envy) — "one without cavil"

anvaya.form: adjective, masculine, accusative plural (agrees with worlds)

anvaya.parts: पुण्य (virtuous) + कर्मन् (deed) — "those whose deeds are virtuous"

verses.explanation: The door opened to its widest: śṛṇuyād api — even one who only *hears*, asking nothing but faith and the absence of sneering. No Sanskrit, no study: the grandmother at the recitation, the child half-listening at the lamp. So 'pi muktaḥ — that one *too* is freed, freed from sin, the commentators say, and reaches the bright worlds of those whose deeds were good. The verse promises a real ascent, not the whole summit: Shankara notes that 'even' implies how much more awaits one who understands, and Ramanuja sees those worlds as places where devotion keeps growing toward release.
verses.connection: Completes the circle of 13.26: the path of the trusting ear, honored to the very end.
verses.reflection: If all you did today was listen without scoffing — that too is counted; even the lowest rung lifts you.
verses.background: The transmission ethic is given: this is not to be spoken to one without austerity or devotion, to the unwilling ear, or the scoffer — but whoever declares this supreme secret among My devotees, showing highest love to Me, shall come to Me without doubt; none does Me dearer service, none on earth shall be dearer. Who studies this dialogue worships Me by the sacrifice of knowledge; even the faithful hearer, free of scoffing, is liberated to the bright worlds.
verses.hook: What does someone gain who only listens to this teaching with faith?

views.text: 'Even' implies that one who knows the meaning hardly needs mention; the freed hearer reaches the worlds of those who performed rites like the Agnihotra.
Hearing from a qualified teacher removes what blocks devotion, and the worlds reached are those of devotees who help the newcomer's devotion grow toward liberation.
Even one who only overhears another's recitation, without finding fault with how it is chanted, is freed from sin and reaches the worlds of the Aśvamedha-performers.
Not everyone can grasp the Gita's depths, but those who merely hear it with faith also benefit, as God notes their sincerity, as seen in Shankaracharya's unlettered but faithful disciple Sananda.

verses.devanagari:
कच्चिदेतच्छ्रुतं पार्थ त्वयैकाग्रेण चेतसा ।
कच्चिदज्ञानसम्मोहः प्रनष्टस्ते धनञ्जय॥
verses.transliteration:
kaccidetacchrutaṃ pārtha tvayaikāgreṇa cetasā
kaccidajñānasammohaḥ pranaṣṭaste dhanañjaya
verses.essence: Has this been heard by you, Partha, with one-pointed mind? Has the delusion of your ignorance been destroyed, Dhananjaya?
verses.translation: Has this been heard, O Arjuna, with one-pointed mind? Has the delusion of thy ignorance been destroyed, O Dhananjaya?

anvaya.parts: एक (one) + अग्र (point) — "fixed on one point"
अज्ञान (ignorance) + सम्मोह (bewilderment) — "bewilderment caused by ignorance"
धन (wealth) + जय (winning) — "one who wins wealth"

verses.explanation: The Teacher turns and asks — kaccit, the gentle interrogative of one who will not presume: did it reach you? whole? The question honors everything 18.63 established: the teaching cannot complete itself; only the hearer's own settled understanding can close the circuit. All of scripture waits, in the end, on one person's honest answer.
verses.connection: The exam of a single question — answered, after eighteen chapters, in 18.73.
verses.reflection: Answer the Teacher's question honestly tonight: did it reach me? Is anything of the fog gone?
verses.background: The Teacher turns to His student with the gentlest of examinations: has this been heard with one-pointed mind, O Partha — has the delusion of your ignorance been destroyed? And Arjuna gives the answer the whole poem exists to reach: destroyed is my delusion; memory is regained, by Your grace, O Achyuta. I stand firm, my doubts are gone — I will act according to Your word.
verses.hook: What does Krishna ask Arjuna once the teaching is finished?

views.text: The question tests whether the pupil has understood, so that if not the teacher can explain another way: the teacher's duty is to bring the student to the goal by whatever means work.
The delusion meant is the one that made Arjuna say 'I shall not fight'.
As a teacher, Krishna checks whether his student has understood, ready to explain again or go into more detail if Arjun is still unclear.

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
नष्टो मोहः स्मृतिर्लब्धा त्वत्प्रसादान्मयाच्युत ।
स्थितोऽस्मि गतसन्देहः करिष्ये वचनं तव॥
verses.transliteration:
naṣṭo mohaḥ smṛtirlabdhā tvatprasādānmayācyuta
sthito'smi gatasandehaḥ kariṣye vacanaṃ tava
verses.essence: Arjuna says: my delusion is destroyed; memory is regained, Achyuta, by your grace. I stand firm, my doubts dispelled. I will act by your word.
verses.translation: Destroyed is my delusion as I have gained my knowledge (memory) through Thy grace, O Krishna. I remain freed from doubts. I will act according to Thy word.

anvaya.form: compound, masculine, ablative singular (from, because of)
anvaya.parts: त्वत् (your) + प्रसाद (grace) — "the grace that is yours"

anvaya.base: गतसन्देह · one whose doubt is gone
anvaya.parts: गत (gone) + सन्देह (doubt) — "one whose doubt has gone"

verses.explanation: The destination of the entire poem, in four clauses: naṣṭo mohaḥ — the delusion that dropped the bow is gone; smṛtir labdhā — *memory regained*, not new information but the self remembered, the exact reversal of 2.63, where memory's loss began the fall; tvat-prasādāt — and he names the real agent: grace. Then the man who sat down stands: sthito 'smi gata-sandehaḥ, doubt gone. Kariṣye vacanaṁ tava — freely, as 18.63 allowed, he chooses the word he was never forced to obey. Not every commentator hears a finished sage: Abhinavagupta reads only a readiness to fight here, with full realisation still ahead.
verses.connection: Chapter 1's collapse answered point for point: the seated weeper stands, the cast-down bow is taken up — by choice.
verses.reflection: Say the four when you are ready — delusion gone, memory regained, standing firm, I will act — and stand.
verses.background: The Teacher turns to His student with the gentlest of examinations: has this been heard with one-pointed mind, O Partha — has the delusion of your ignorance been destroyed? And Arjuna gives the answer the whole poem exists to reach: destroyed is my delusion; memory is regained, by Your grace, O Achyuta. I stand firm, my doubts are gone — I will act according to Your word.
verses.hook: How does Arjuna answer once his confusion is gone?

views.text: The whole fruit of the scripture is just this: delusion born of ignorance destroyed and memory of the Self regained. 'I will do your word' means no duty remains for him.
The delusion was taking the self for the body and missing that all things are the Lord's body; smṛti is knowing things as they are, including that duties done for the Lord do not bind.
Only an inclination to fight has arisen; full realisation of Brahman is not yet born in Arjuna, which leaves room for the later Anugītā.
'I stand' means I stand ready for battle; the doubt that has gone is the doubt about what dharma requires.

Arjun, once grief-stricken, now stands firm and ready to do Krishna's will, crediting grace rather than the lecture alone; spiritual knowledge is received through grace, faith and humility, not proud evaluation.

verses.speaker: सञ्जय उवाच
verses.devanagari:
इत्यहं वासुदेवस्य पार्थस्य च महात्मनः ।
संवादमिममश्रौषमद्भुतं रोमहर्षणम्॥
verses.transliteration:
ityahaṃ vāsudevasya pārthasya ca mahātmanaḥ
saṃvādamimamaśrauṣamadbhutaṃ romaharṣaṇam
verses.essence: Sanjaya says: thus did I hear this wondrous dialogue of Vasudeva and the great-souled Partha — causing my hair to stand on end.
verses.translation: Thus I have heard this wonderful dialogue between Krishna and the high-souled Arjuna, which causes the hair to stand on end.

anvaya.base: thus (marks a quotation or a reason)

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + आत्मन् (self, soul) — "one whose soul is great"

anvaya.meaning: making the hair stand on end
anvaya.parts: रोमन् (body hair) + हर्षण (making bristle) — "that makes the hair bristle"

verses.explanation: The frame returns for the last time: Sanjaya, the seer-narrator, closing the frame the blind king opened with his question at 1.1. His word for the whole: adbhutam roma-harṣaṇam — a wonder that raises the hair. We are reminded that everything since 'dharma-kṣetre' has passed through this one listening witness to a blind king — and now through him to us.
verses.connection: The outer frame closes: the epilogue of the witness (18.74–78) begins.
verses.reflection: Be a faithful Sanjaya today: carry one true conversation to someone who could not be in the room.
verses.background: The outer frame closes: Sanjaya, hair thrilling, tells the blind king what he has heard — this wondrous dialogue of Vasudeva and the great-souled Partha, received by Vyasa's grace from the Lord of yoga Himself — and confesses that remembering it again and again, and that most wondrous form, he rejoices again and again. His settled conviction ends the Gita: where Krishna the Lord of yoga is, and Partha the bowman, there are fortune, victory, prosperity, and unshakable right.
verses.hook: How does Sanjaya feel after hearing the whole dialogue?

views.text: Sañjaya says he heard this unique, extremely wonderful conversation between Vāsudeva and the great-souled Pārtha, which makes the hair stand on end.
Calls Arjuna great-souled because he has great understanding and has taken refuge at Krishna's feet.
The dialogue is wondrous because it concerns the hidden, immortal Self; hair standing on end is the sign of higher emotion that devotees often know.
Sanjay ends his narration amazed, calling Arjun great-souled for heeding Krishna; his hair standing on end is a classic sign of intense devotional fervour.

Vyasa gave Sanjaya divine sight and hearing; Sanjaya says this to make his account credible to the king.
By the grace of his guru Vyasa, Sanjay was given the clairvoyance to witness Kurukshetra from the palace, and Vyasa, hearing both conversations, compiled them into the Gita.

verses.reflection: Return to one passage that moved you and let it move you again — joy renews at each remembering.

views.text: Recollecting again and again Hari's greatly extraordinary Cosmic form, Sañjaya tells the King he is struck with great wonder and rejoices repeatedly.
The form is the sovereign form shown to Arjuna, which Sanjaya too saw directly; joy from remembering it stirs his amazement.
Sanjay too saw the rare cosmic form as narrator of the divine pastime; such unexpected grace, used well, speeds spiritual progress, and he keeps contemplating it in a current of devotion.

धनुस् (bow) + धर (holder) — "one who holds the bow"

anvaya.form: adjective, feminine, nominative singular (agrees with right conduct)

verses.explanation: The Gita's last verse, and the tradition's benediction ever since: not a doctrine but a *conjunction* — yatra... yatra... tatra: where the Lord of yoga and the bow-bearing human stand together, there are fortune, victory, abundance and unfailing right conduct. Grace alone does not fight; effort alone does not see; joined, they are invincible. The blind king asked at 1.1 what happened on the field of dharma. Sanjaya's last words answer with where to place one's hope — and, Śrīdhara adds, with a plea to the king himself: the winning side is already plain. Wherever those two ride in one chariot — any heart, on any morning — dhruvā nītir matir mama: this is my settled conviction.
verses.connection: The closing benediction: divine guidance and human resolve in one chariot — the whole Gita compressed into its final image, answering the question of 1.1.
verses.reflection: Close with the benediction's geometry: put the divine and your own bow in one chariot today — and trust the outcome.

His settled conviction ends the Gita: where Krishna the Lord of yoga is, and Partha the bowman, there are fortune, victory, prosperity, and unshakable right.
verses.hook: Where do victory, prosperity and justice always abide?

refs.note: Declares that none is equal to God and none greater, supporting the verdict that victory always lies with the Lord and his devotee.

views.text: Krishna is Lord of yoga as the source from which all yogas arise; 'where' means the side on which he and Arjuna with the Gāṇḍīva stand, the Pandava side.
Krishna rules all of nature, on whose will every thing's being and action depends; Arjuna is the one who took sole refuge at his feet, and such places always hold fortune and sound morality.
Steady recollection of the dialogue's meaning, deepened into direct undivided cognition, is what leads to Brahman; fortune and victory follow from that.
Sanjaya's hint to the king: even now, take refuge in Krishna, make peace with the Pandavas and save your sons' lives.
Counting armies is irrelevant: victory, goodness and abundance always side with God and his surrendered devotee, through whom his incomparable glory shines and falsehood is overcome.
